title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
text: Methodological guidelines and implementation templates for survival analysis, delayed treatment initiation, and target trial emulation in health technology assessment.

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 1 Introduction: Causal Inference in Time-to-Event Data
text:
1 Introduction: Causal Inference in Time-to-Event Data
In health technology assessment (HTA), clinical endpoints are frequently time-to-event outcomes. While aggregate summaries like Overall Survival (OS) or Progression-Free Survival (PFS) are represented as curves showing the proportion or probability of surviving patients at specific points in time, the underlying outcome measured at the patient level is the actual duration of time (e.g., months or days) elapsed from a defined baseline (such as diagnosis or treatment initiation) until the clinical event of interest (e.g., death, relapse) occurs.
Unlike binary outcomes where logistic regression or propensity score matching are applied statically, survival data introduces a critical dimension: Time.
If time-to-event analysis is not bounded by strict causal constraints, observational analyses can yield severe selection biases. A primary methodological challenge in retrospective registries is Immortal Time Bias (ITB).

1.1 The Coffee & Heart Disease Paradox: Temporal Ordering and Selection Bias
To understand why a strict time-to-event framework is necessary, consider the “Coffee & Heart Disease Paradox”:

The Paradox: Observational studies often show that coffee drinkers have lower rates of heart disease than non-coffee drinkers (Hazard Ratio < 1.0).
The Reverse Causality: In reality, patients who develop heart symptoms or are diagnosed with high risk are advised by doctors to quit coffee.
The Methodological Connection: If we classify exposure statically based on whether a patient drinks coffee during follow-up, we violate the chronological ordering of causal inference. A patient who develops heart disease on Day 50 and subsequently quits coffee will be misclassified as a “non-coffee drinker” at the end of the study. This attributes their heart event (which occurred before quitting) to the non-exposure group, violating the non-anticipatory constraint of time-to-event outcomes.

To resolve this paradox, we must align the study baseline (\(T_0\)), measure confounders (like baseline heart risk) strictly before exposure initiation, and model exposure dynamically over time. This is exactly what Target Trial Emulation and Time-Varying survival models achieve.

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
text:
2 The Target Trial Emulation (TTE) Framework
Target Trial Emulation is a structured design framework developed by Miguel Hernán and colleagues to guide the design and analysis of observational studies. The core principle is that we should design our observational study to mimic a hypothetical randomized trial as closely as possible.

2.1 The 7 Dimensions of the Target Trial Approach
According to the official NICE RWE Framework (Section 5.2)1, a target trial must be defined across 7 core dimensions to prevent bias and ensure transparency:
1 Official Source: NICE Real-World Evidence Framework (2022), Section 5.2 (“The target trial approach”). Methodological Reference: Hernán MA, Robins JM (2016). Using Big Data to Emulate a Target Trial When a Randomized Trial Is Not Available. Am J Epidemiol.







Dimension
NICE RWE Framework Requirement
Application to Survival Cohorts




1. Eligibility criteria
Define clear inclusion/exclusion criteria at baseline.
Patients must meet all criteria at Time Zero (\(T_0\)), ensuring no baseline selection bias.


2. Treatment strategies
Specify the interventions being compared.
Arm A: Initiate active treatment within a defined window. Arm B: Initiate Standard of Care (SOC) / no treatment.


3. Assignment procedure
Define how treatment groups are formed.
Emulate randomization at \(T_0\) using Propensity Scores (IPTW or matching) based on baseline covariates.


4. Follow-up period
Align follow-up start exactly with \(T_0\).
Clock starts ticking for all patients at \(T_0\). Ends at the event, death, censoring, or study end.


5. Outcomes
Define a standardized clinical endpoint.
First occurrence of the event (e.g., death, progression) during the follow-up period.


6. Causal effect of interest
Specify the causal contrast of interest.
Intention-to-Treat (ITT): Effect of treatment assignment at \(T_0\), regardless of later compliance.


7. Analysis plan
Specify the statistical estimator.
Cox Proportional Hazards model or parametric survival models, adjusted for baseline confounding.





2.2 Deep Dive: The New User Design
A fundamental rule of TTE is the New User Design2. In observational studies, researchers often mistakenly compare “prevalent users” (patients already on the drug for some time) with “never users.” This introduces three major issues:
2 Defining a “New User”: A patient is classified as a “new user” only if they initiate the drug of interest for the first time at \(T_0\). This requires establishing a washout period (e.g., 180 or 365 days prior to \(T_0\)) during which they have no records of the drug in the database, ensuring they are not “prevalent users.”
Survivor Bias: Prevalent users are, by definition, “survivors” who have tolerated the drug and survived long enough to be observed in the database. Patients who died or discontinued the drug early due to adverse events are systematically excluded from the treated group, creating a false survival advantage.
Baseline Contamination: To adjust for confounding, we must measure covariates before treatment starts. For prevalent users, their baseline measurements (e.g., blood pressure, lab values) are already affected by the treatment, making it impossible to measure their true pre-treatment state.
\(T_0\) Synchronization: We cannot align the start of follow-up with the start of treatment if treatment began years before the observation period.

A New User Design enforces that patients are only entered into the cohort at the exact moment they initiate the treatment of interest.


2.3 Deep Dive: Intention-to-Treat (ITT) in RWD (Cloning & Censoring)
In randomized trials, the ITT principle analyzes patients in the group they were randomized to, regardless of whether they complied. In retrospective RWD, we often face a “grace period”—a window of time (e.g., 30 or 60 days) after diagnosis during which patients are allowed to initiate treatment.
If we assign patients to the “treated” group because they initiated treatment on day 30, we violate the ITT principle by using “future knowledge” at \(T_0\). To solve this, TTE uses Cloning:

Cloning at \(T_0\): At the moment of eligibility (\(T_0\)), we create two identical copies of each patient. One copy is assigned to Arm A (Initiate Treatment), and one copy is assigned to Arm B (Standard of Care).
Follow-up: Both clones begin follow-up at \(T_0\).
Censoring: If a patient assigned to Arm B initiates treatment on day 30, their Arm B clone is censored at day 30 (because they violated the “no treatment” protocol). The Arm A clone continues to be followed.
IPCW Adjustment: To correct for selection bias introduced by this artificial censoring, we apply Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights (IPCW), which upweights the remaining uncensored clones who share similar baseline characteristics.



2.4 Causal Transparency: Why TTE Aligns with the DataSAT Tool
NICE prefers TTE because it enforces Transparency.
In a simple Cox regression, you often see: \[\text{Surv}(\text{time}, \text{event}) \sim \text{Treatment} + \text{Confounders}\]
An auditor cannot see:

When was the treatment started?
Were the confounders measured before or after the drug was given?
Is there a “Healthy User Bias”?

By using the DataSAT tool (Data Suitability Assessment Tool), NICE auditors look for Provenance—the clear lineage of how a patient moved from a raw database record to a study row. TTE forces the researcher to write a “Trial Protocol” before touching the data, making it obvious where \(T_0\) is. If an auditor sees that you measured covariates after the drug was given and used them as baseline, the TTE framework will flag this as a “Post-baseline Bias” immediately.

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 3 HTA Case Study: Drug X (METex14) Case Study
text:
3 HTA Case Study: Drug X (METex14) Case Study
To see how these principles apply to a real submission, we examine the case of Drug X, a precision oncology therapy for METex14-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

3.1 Case Overview: The Drug X Conflict

The Innovation: Due to the rarity of the METex14 mutation and ethical constraints, only a Single-arm Trial (N=40) was conducted for Drug X.
The Objection: The Evidence Assessment Group (EAG) flagged the submission as “high risk” because there was no randomized head-to-head comparison. Natural history for METex14 is aggressive, and simple benchmarking is insufficient.
The Strategy: We leverage the UK Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) database to construct an External Control Arm (ECA) of 200 patients, using the Target Trial Emulation (TTE) framework to satisfy NICE’s demand for rigorous causal inference.



3.2 Step 1: Data Suitability Audit (DataSAT)
According to Sections 3.1–3.3 of the NICE RWE Framework, we must prove the data is fit for purpose across three core dimensions:








Dimension
HTA Audit Response (HES Database)
NICE Framework Requirement




Provenance
Data sourced from NHS Digital with a clear audit trail from ICD-10 coding to the final analytical dataset.
Evaluate the origin and trustworthiness of data sources, methods of collection, and governance. (Section 3.1)


Quality
METex14 status confirmed via secondary linkage to SACT and genomic records; completeness checked for key covariates.
Assess the completeness and accuracy of eligibility criteria, exposures, and outcomes. (Section 3.2)


Relevance
HES covers 99% of NHS hospital activity, matching the SOC pathways in the UK.
Ensure findings generalise to the target population and clinical care pathways in the NHS. (Section 3.3)





3.3 Defining \(T_0\) (Zero-time Alignment)
To avoid Immortal Time Bias, we align \(T_0\) as the moment a patient meets all eligibility criteria AND is assigned to treatment (Section 5.2).

3.3.1 Why Immortal Time Bias is a “Statistical Killer”

Logic Paradox: In RWD studies, patients from diagnosis to actual treatment initiation (Drug X) face delays (e.g., 1 month). If follow-up begins at diagnosis, but grouping is based on whether they ever received treatment, the period before receiving the drug is immortal—if the patient died on Day 15, they would never have lived long enough to receive the drug, and would automatically be classified into the control group.
Case Simulation:

Patient A: Diagnosed Jan 1, scheduled for Drug X, dies Jan 15 (unexposed). Classified as Control.
Patient B: Diagnosed Jan 1, initiates Drug X Feb 1, survives until June.
Result: The Drug Y/X group artificially filters out those who die before drug administration, inflating the active group’s survival.

TTE Surgery: The clock must start ticking exactly at treatment initiation, or grace periods must be modeled using cloning.



3.3.2 The Control Arm \(T_0\)
Where does the control arm’s \(T_0\) start if they never receive the active treatment?

Synchronicity Principle: \(T_0\) is the moment the patient meets all clinical eligibility criteria (e.g., METex14 diagnosis + ECOG status).
Timeline Alignment:

Incorrect: Treated group starts at “first drug administration”, while controls start at “diagnosis”. This gives the treated group an implicit survival benefit.
Correct TTE Approach: Both groups start follow-up at the exact date they meet all eligibility criteria (the clinical decision point, or clinical equipoise).




3.3.3 Handling the Grace Period
In RWD, a patient has a “window” of time (grace period) to initiate treatment (e.g., 30 days after diagnosis).

If a patient initiates treatment on Day 20, they contribute 20 days of “unexposed” person-time to the control group.
Using cloning, we create two clones at diagnosis. The “Control Clone” is followed until Day 20, where it is censored because the patient initiated treatment. The “Treated Clone” starts contributing treated time from Day 20 onwards.




3.4 Step 2: Cloning & Censoring Mechanics
To maintain ITT principles:

Anti-Future-Knowledge: We cannot look ahead to see what the patient did. We clone them at \(T_0\) into both paths.
Artificial Censoring: If the patient’s actual path deviates from a clone’s assigned arm, that clone is censored.
IPCW Weighting: Because censoring might be non-random, we estimate the probability of being censored at time \(t\) based on baseline covariates and apply Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights to the remaining patients, dynamically restoring the balance.

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 4 Immortal Time Bias (ITB): Theory & Landmark Analysis
text:
4 Immortal Time Bias (ITB): Theory & Landmark Analysis

4.1 The Meditation & Longevity Paradox
Consider a study evaluating whether a 12-week intensive meditation course increases overall survival (OS):

Cohort: 1,000 participants followed for 5 years.
Exposure Group (\(Z=1\)): Completed the full 12-week program.
Control Group (\(Z=0\)): Did not complete the program (includes those who died or dropped out before week 12).
The Result: Participants who completed the course show a Hazard Ratio (\(HR\)) of 0.30 (70% risk reduction).3
The Error: Since a patient had to survive 12 weeks to complete the program, the meditation group is guaranteed 0% mortality during the first 12 weeks. Sicker patients who died in weeks 1–11 were automatically allocated to the control group.

3 Completion status at Week 12 is post-baseline information. It cannot be used retrospectively to define the baseline exposure group; otherwise, the first 12 weeks of survival are incorrectly credited to the intervention.

4.2 Landmark Analysis
Landmark Analysis is a classical approach to resolve this:

Select Landmark Time (\(T_L\)): E.g., Week 12.
Exclude Early Events: Exclude all patients who died or were censored before \(T_L\).
Re-classify: Classify survivors at \(T_L\) based on their exposure status at \(T_L\).
Follow-up: Set \(T_L\) as the new baseline (\(T_{start} = T_L\)) and follow patients from that point.


HTA Audit of Landmark Analysis

Pros: Simple, highly intuitive, and removes the immortal period.
Cons:

Information Loss: Discards all events and person-time before \(T_L\). If the drug has high early toxicity, this signal is completely lost.
Selection Bias: The populations at \(T_L\) may no longer be balanced, as sicker patients in the control group may have died, while sicker patients in the treated group were protected by the “immortal” definition.


Therefore, landmark analysis is usually better positioned as an intuitive diagnostic or sensitivity analysis, rather than the preferred primary analysis for HTA submissions. It is most defensible when the clinical question is explicitly conditional on surviving and remaining eligible until the landmark time; otherwise, time-varying exposure models or cloning-censoring-IPCW are generally more aligned with the original target trial estimand.

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
text:
6 Time-Dependent Cox Model & HTA Practice
The time-dependent Cox model is an extension of the standard Cox proportional hazards model that allows a patient’s treatment status to change during follow-up. This makes it useful for auditing and correcting immortal time bias when treatment initiation is delayed.

6.1 What the Model Does
In a standard Cox model, treatment is usually treated as fixed at baseline:
\[
h_i(t) = h_0(t)\exp(\beta Z_i + \gamma L_i)
\]
where \(Z_i\) is a single treatment indicator for patient \(i\), and \(L_i\) represents baseline covariates such as age or ECOG status.
The problem is that delayed treatment is not fixed at baseline. A patient may be untreated from Day 0 to Day 60, then treated from Day 60 onward. A time-dependent Cox model replaces the fixed treatment indicator \(Z_i\) with a time-updated treatment indicator \(Z_i(t)\):
\[
h_i(t) = h_0(t)\exp(\beta Z_i(t) + \gamma L_i)
\]
Here, \(Z_i(t)=0\) before treatment starts and \(Z_i(t)=1\) after treatment starts. At each event time, the Cox model compares patients according to their treatment status at that moment, not according to information observed later in follow-up.
This is the key correction for immortal time bias: the waiting period before treatment is counted as untreated person-time, rather than being retrospectively assigned to the treated group.


6.2 Counting Process Data Structure
To estimate this model, the data usually need to be written in counting process format. Rather than one row per patient, the dataset is split into multiple intervals (tstart, tstop] where treatment status remains constant.

Start-Stop Data Format Example (Patient #101)
Patient #101 has a treatment initiation lag of 60 days and dies on Day 500. We split this patient’s record into two lines:










Patient ID
Start (Day)
Stop (Day)
Status (Event)
Treatment (\(Z\))




#101
0
60
0 (Alive)
0 (Not treated)


#101
60
500
1 (Death)
1 (Treated)



At Day 60, the patient’s treatment status switches from not treated to treated. The patient is not removed from follow-up; instead, their contribution to the risk set is updated from untreated person-time to treated person-time.






NoteWhy This Is Not Duplicating the Patient





In a Cox model, the partial likelihood is built at each observed event time. At each event time, the model rebuilds the risk set: who is still alive, still under follow-up, and what are their covariate values at that moment?
In a standard Cox model, treatment status is fixed, so the model always reads the same \(Z_i\) for patient \(i\). In a time-dependent Cox model, the model reads \(Z_i(t)\), meaning the patient’s treatment status at the event time being evaluated.
For Patient #101, this means:

before Day 60, the patient can enter risk sets as Z = 0;
after Day 60, the same patient can enter risk sets as Z = 1;
at no event time do both rows enter the same risk set simultaneously.

The two rows therefore represent two non-overlapping risk intervals for the same patient, not two independent patients. The patient contributes untreated person-time before Day 60, treated person-time after Day 60, and one death event at Day 500.






6.3 Landmark vs. Time-Dependent Cox








Dimension
Time-dependent Cox
Landmark Analysis




Data Retention
Retains all patients and events from Day 0.
Discards patients/events prior to Landmark \(T_L\).


Causal Question
Causal effect starting from Day 0.
Conditional effect given survival to \(T_L\).


Early Toxicity
Captures early adverse event signals.
Masked if events occur before \(T_L\).


HTA Audit Preference
Preferred for primary analysis.
Used primarily as a sensitivity analysis.





6.4 Applying the Time-Dependent Cox Model
We now restructure the same simulated cohort into counting process format using tmerge().

df_tv <- tmerge(df, df, id = id, event = event(time, event))

# 2. Merge the time-dependent treatment initiation event
df_tv <- tmerge(df_tv, df, id = id, treatment_status = tdc(t_init))

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
text:
7 R Simulation: Validation of Estimators
We simulate a cohort of 500 patients where treatment initiation is delayed due to an administrative “Approval Lag.”

7.1 Simulating the Cohort and Biased Analysis
We simulate a true treatment Hazard Ratio of 0.70 (30% risk reduction). Age and ECOG status act as baseline confounders.


R Code
library(survival)
library(EValue)
set.seed(42)
n <- 500

# Helper function to render Cox model summaries as kable tables
show_cox <- function(fit, caption) {
  sum_fit <- summary(fit)
  coefs <- sum_fit$coefficients
  cis <- sum_fit$conf.int
  se_col <- if ("robust se" %in% colnames(coefs)) "robust se" else "se(coef)"
  z_col <- if ("z" %in% colnames(coefs)) "z" else colnames(coefs)[4]
  tbl <- data.frame(
    Covariate = rownames(coefs),
    `Hazard Ratio` = round(coefs[, "exp(coef)"], 4),
    `Log HR (coef)` = round(coefs[, "coef"], 4),
    `Std Error` = round(coefs[, se_col], 4),
    `z-value` = round(coefs[, z_col], 3),
    `p-value` = format.pval(coefs[, "Pr(>|z|)"], digits = 4),
    `95% LCL` = round(cis[, 3], 4),
    `95% UCL` = round(cis[, 4], 4),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  knitr::kable(tbl, caption = caption, align = "lrrrrrrr")
}

# 1. Simulate Baseline Confounders
age <- rnorm(n, mean = 60, sd = 10)
ecog <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)

# 2. Simulate Treatment Selection (Confounding by Indication)
# Sicker (ECOG=1) and older patients are more likely to receive treatment
ps_prob <- plogis(-1.5 + 0.02 * age + 0.5 * ecog)
z_treatment <- rbinom(n, 1, ps_prob)

# For those treated, add a random initiation delay between 30 and 120 days
t_init <- ifelse(z_treatment == 1, runif(n, 30, 120), Inf)

# 3. Simulate Survival Times (True treatment HR = 0.70)
true_hr <- 0.70
lambda_base <- 0.001 * exp(0.02 * age + 0.5 * ecog)

u <- runif(n)
log_u <- -log(u)

t_event <- numeric(n)
for(i in 1:n) {
  l0 <- lambda_base[i]
  l1 <- l0 * true_hr
  t_tr <- t_init[i]
  
  if (log_u[i] <= l0 * t_tr) {
    t_event[i] <- log_u[i] / l0
  } else {
    t_event[i] <- t_tr + (log_u[i] - l0 * t_tr) / l1
  }
}

# Censoring between 150 and 730 days
t_censor <- runif(n, 150, 730)
time <- pmin(t_event, t_censor)
event <- as.integer(t_event <= t_censor)

df <- data.frame(id = 1:n, age, ecog, z_treatment, t_init, time, event)

# Determine treatment status based on actual follow-up (Biased approach)
df$ever_treated <- ifelse(df$t_init < df$time, 1, 0)

# --- Biased Analysis: Static Cox Model ---
fit_biased <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ ever_treated + age + ecog, data = df)
show_cox(fit_biased, "Biased Static Cox Proportional Hazards Model Results (Immortal Time Unadjusted)")

7.2 Method 1: Landmark Analysis (Day 90)
We apply Landmark Analysis at Day 90:


R Code
t_landmark <- 90

# Exclude patients who died or were censored before Day 90
df_landmark <- df[df$time > t_landmark, ]

# Classify status at Landmark
df_landmark$treated_at_landmark <- ifelse(df_landmark$t_init <= t_landmark, 1, 0)

# Shift time
df_landmark$time_shifted <- df_landmark$time - t_landmark

fit_landmark <- coxph(Surv(time_shifted, event) ~ treated_at_landmark + age + ecog, data = df_landmark)
show_cox(fit_landmark, "Landmark Analysis (Day 90) Cox Proportional Hazards Model Results")

7.4 Method 3: Cloning-Censoring-IPCW Analysis
We now emulate a strategy-level target trial with a 90-day grace period:

Strategy 1: initiate Drug X within 90 days of diagnosis.
Strategy 0: do not initiate Drug X within 90 days of diagnosis.

Each patient is cloned into both strategies. A clone is artificially censored when the observed treatment path becomes incompatible with its assigned strategy.


R Code
grace_period <- 90

# 1. Clone each patient into both treatment strategies
df_clone <- rbind(
  transform(df, strategy = 1, strategy_label = "Initiate within 90 days"),
  transform(df, strategy = 0, strategy_label = "No initiation within 90 days")
)

# 2. Define artificial censoring rules
df_clone$artificial_censor_time <- Inf

# Strategy 1 violation: no treatment initiation by the end of the grace period
df_clone$artificial_censor_time[
  df_clone$strategy == 1 &
    df_clone$t_init > grace_period &
    df_clone$time > grace_period
] <- grace_period

# Strategy 0 violation: treatment initiation during the grace period
df_clone$artificial_censor_time[
  df_clone$strategy == 0 &
    df_clone$t_init <= grace_period &
    df_clone$t_init < df_clone$time
] <- df_clone$t_init[
  df_clone$strategy == 0 &
    df_clone$t_init <= grace_period &
    df_clone$t_init < df_clone$time
]

# 3. Observed follow-up under each assigned strategy
df_clone$obs_time <- pmin(df_clone$time, df_clone$artificial_censor_time)
df_clone$outcome_event <- as.integer(df_clone$event == 1 & df_clone$time <= df_clone$artificial_censor_time)
df_clone$artificial_censored <- as.integer(df_clone$artificial_censor_time < df_clone$time)
df_clone$uncensored <- 1 - df_clone$artificial_censored

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
text:
8 Causal Evidence Reconciliation
An estimand means the exact causal question being estimated. The methods below all address delayed treatment initiation, but they do not answer precisely the same question:

Naive static Cox asks a biased future-informed question: did patients who eventually received Drug X survive longer than those who did not?
Landmark analysis estimates a conditional effect among patients who survived and remained observable until Day 90.
Time-dependent Cox estimates the hazard contrast associated with current treatment status at each event time.
Cloning-censoring-IPCW estimates a strategy contrast, such as “initiate Drug X within 90 days” versus “do not initiate within 90 days,” starting from the original eligibility date.

The table below summarizes the estimates across the four analyses compared with the true simulated treatment effect.


R Code
# Extract statistics
hr_biased  <- exp(coef(fit_biased)["ever_treated"])
se_biased  <- summary(fit_biased)$coefficients["ever_treated", "se(coef)"]

hr_land    <- exp(coef(fit_landmark)["treated_at_landmark"])
se_land    <- summary(fit_landmark)$coefficients["treated_at_landmark", "se(coef)"]

hr_tv      <- exp(coef(fit_tv)["treatment_status"])
se_tv      <- summary(fit_tv)$coefficients["treatment_status", "se(coef)"]

hr_ipcw    <- exp(coef(fit_ipcw)["strategy"])
se_ipcw    <- summary(fit_ipcw)$coefficients["strategy", "robust se"]

# Combine into reconciliation matrix
reconciliation_tbl <- data.frame(
  Estimator = c("Ground Truth (True Parameter)", "Biased Model (Static Baseline)", "Landmark Analysis (Day 90)", "Time-Dependent Cox Model", "Cloning-Censoring-IPCW"),
  "Hazard Ratio (HR)" = c(true_hr, hr_biased, hr_land, hr_tv, hr_ipcw),
  "Standard Error" = c(NA, se_biased, se_land, se_tv, se_ipcw),
  "95% LCL" = c(NA, exp(confint(fit_biased)["ever_treated", 1]), exp(confint(fit_landmark)["treated_at_landmark", 1]), exp(confint(fit_tv)["treatment_status", 1]), exp(confint(fit_ipcw)["strategy", 1])),
  "95% UCL" = c(NA, exp(confint(fit_biased)["ever_treated", 2]), exp(confint(fit_landmark)["treated_at_landmark", 2]), exp(confint(fit_tv)["treatment_status", 2]), exp(confint(fit_ipcw)["strategy", 2])),
  "Bias vs. Truth (Log HR)" = c(0.0000, coef(fit_biased)["ever_treated"] - log(true_hr), coef(fit_landmark)["treated_at_landmark"] - log(true_hr), coef(fit_tv)["treatment_status"] - log(true_hr), coef(fit_ipcw)["strategy"] - log(true_hr)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 9 Quantitative Bias Analysis: E-Value Sensitivity Analysis
text:
9 Quantitative Bias Analysis: E-Value Sensitivity Analysis
When submitting RWE to HTA bodies, we must audit the robustness of our findings against unmeasured confounding. We compute the E-value for the time-dependent Cox Hazard Ratio (\(HR = 0.693\)).

9.1 E-Value Math & Formula Setup
The E-value is defined as the minimum strength of association on the risk ratio scale that an unmeasured confounder (\(U\)) must have with both: 1. The treatment assignment (\(Z\)) 2. The clinical outcome (\(Y\))
to fully explain away the observed treatment-outcome association.
The formula depends on the cumulative incidence of the outcome:

Rare Outcome Assumption (cumulative incidence < 15%):
The Hazard Ratio approximates the Relative Risk (\(RR \approx HR\)). For protective effects (\(HR < 1.0\)), we first invert the HR (\(HR^* = 1 / HR\)) to get a value \(> 1.0\): \[\text{E-value} = HR^* + \sqrt{HR^* \cdot (HR^* - 1)}\]
Common Outcome Correction (cumulative incidence > 15%):
The rare outcome assumption is violated, and we must apply the square root approximation: \[RR \approx \sqrt{HR}\] The corresponding E-value is calculated as: \[\text{E-value} = \sqrt{HR^*} + \sqrt{\sqrt{HR^*} \cdot (\sqrt{HR^*} - 1)}\]

In our cohort, 379 out of 500 patients (75.8%) experienced the event, meaning the outcome is common. We must apply the common outcome correction.


R Code
# 1. Extract HR and confidence limits from the time-varying Cox model
hr_est_val <- exp(coef(fit_tv)["treatment_status"])
hr_lcl_val <- exp(confint(fit_tv)["treatment_status", 1])
hr_ucl_val <- exp(confint(fit_tv)["treatment_status", 2])

# 2. Compute E-value (common outcome correction: rare = FALSE)
ev_survival <- evalues.HR(est = hr_est_val, lo = hr_lcl_val, hi = hr_ucl_val, rare = FALSE)
ev_survival_df <- as.data.frame(ev_survival)

# 3. Format E-value table
ev_survival_tbl <- data.frame(
  "Metric / Parameter" = c("Hazard Ratio (HR)", "E-value (Treatment Effect Bound)"),
  "Point Estimate" = c(sprintf("%.3f", ev_survival_df["HR", "point"]), sprintf("%.3f", ev_survival_df["E-values", "point"])),
  "95% CI Lower Bound" = c(sprintf("%.3f", ev_survival_df["HR", "lower"]), sprintf("%.3f", ev_survival_df["E-values", "lower"])),
  "95% CI Upper Bound" = c(sprintf("%.3f", ev_survival_df["HR", "upper"]), "N/A"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

The point estimate E-value of 1.899 means that an unmeasured confounder would need to increase the probability of treatment assignment by 1.899-fold and increase the hazard of death by 1.899-fold to fully explain away the observed survival benefit.


9.2 Algebraic Derivation of the E-Value (VanderWeele & Ding 2016)
To understand the mathematical strength of the E-value, we trace its algebraic derivation from the Bias Factor model.
Let \(U\) be a binary unmeasured confounder. The observed relative risk \(RR_{obs}\) is related to the true relative risk \(RR_{true}\) by: \[RR_{obs} = RR_{true} \times \text{Bias}\]
where the Bias Factor is defined as: \[\text{Bias} = \frac{RR_{ZU} \times RR_{UY}}{RR_{ZU} + RR_{UY} - 1}\]
Here:

\(RR_{ZU}\) is the risk ratio associating the treatment \(Z\) with the unmeasured confounder \(U\).
\(RR_{UY}\) is the risk ratio associating the unmeasured confounder \(U\) with the outcome \(Y\).

To explain away an observed effect (i.e., to show that the true effect is null, \(RR_{true} = 1.0\)), the Bias Factor must equal or exceed the observed relative risk: \[\text{Bias} \ge RR_{obs}\]
To find the minimum strength of association required for both relationships, we define a single threshold \(E = RR_{ZU} = RR_{UY}\). Substituting \(E\) into the Bias formula: \[\frac{E^2}{2E - 1} \ge RR_{obs}\]
This can be rearranged into a quadratic inequality: \[E^2 - 2RR_{obs} \cdot E + RR_{obs} \ge 0\]
Solving the quadratic equation \(E^2 - 2RR_{obs} \cdot E + RR_{obs} = 0\) using the quadratic formula: \[E = \frac{2RR_{obs} \pm \sqrt{4RR_{obs}^2 - 4RR_{obs}}}{2} = RR_{obs} + \sqrt{RR_{obs}(RR_{obs} - 1)}\]
This is the exact mathematical derivation of the E-value formula. It represents the absolute minimum joint relationship required for an unmeasured confounder to explain away the observed treatment effect.

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
text:
10 HTA Audit & Interview Guide

10.1 Interview Audit Checklist
When auditing a manufacturer’s RWE survival submission (or preparing for an HTA interview), follow these three key checks:

Zero-time Alignment Check:

Question: Identify the exact calendar date of \(T_0\) for both cohorts. Is \(T_0\) defined by the clinical event (diagnosis) or the administrative event (first prescription)?
Audit Rule: Follow-up must start for both cohorts when they meet the eligibility criteria. If the treated group follow-up starts at drug initiation and controls start at diagnosis, the analysis is invalid.

Immortal Time Bias Screen:

Question: Check the initial segment of the Kaplan-Meier curve. Does the treated arm show a “zero-risk” flat line at the start of follow-up?
Audit Rule: A flat line on the treatment curve indicates that patients who died early were excluded from the treated group, indicating Immortal Time Bias.

Statistical Correction Audit:

Question: If a treatment initiation lag exists, was it addressed using a time-varying covariate or a Landmark approach?
Audit Rule: Standard Cox models using a static baseline treatment indicator are statistically invalid in the presence of treatment initiation delays.




10.2 Expert HTA Articulation
Use the following professional statements to articulate survival analysis defense strategies during HTA reviews or interviews:

Justifying Time-Varying Cox Models Over Static Models: > “To prevent the introduction of lead-time and immortal time biases, we did not define treatment statically at baseline based on retrospective treatment status. Instead, we modeled treatment as a time-varying exposure using a counting process framework with start-stop intervals via the tmerge protocol. This ensures that the risk sets are updated dynamically at each event time, preventing the misattribution of waiting-period survival to the active drug’s efficacy.”
Defending the Conditional Exchangeability Assumption: > “Second, to maintain conditional exchangeability over time despite treatment delays, we utilized a cloning-and-censoring approach with IPCW, ensuring the counterfactual baseline characteristics remained balanced as the retrospective follow-up progressed.”
Empirically Validating the Positivity Assumption: > “Finally, we empirically validated the positivity assumption by confirming that patients across all covariate strata in our HES data had a non-zero probability of receiving standard of care, preventing structurally empty cells in our propensity score distributions.”
Defending against Unmeasured Confounding via E-Values: > “Although our real-world registry lacks smoking history, our E-value of 1.70 demonstrates that to nullify the observed survival benefit, an unmeasured confounder would need to increase both the likelihood of treatment and the hazard of death by at least 1.70-fold. This is larger than the hazard associated with major clinical indicators like age in our adjusted models, making it highly implausible that a missing confounder of this magnitude exists that is completely independent of the clinical variables adjusted for in our primary analysis.”

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
text: Bridging the Gap Between Observational Real-World Data and Causal Claims in HTA

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
section: 1 Introduction: The Confounding Challenge & Self-Selection Bias
text:
1 Introduction: The Confounding Challenge & Self-Selection Bias
In observational studies, treatment assignment (\(D\)) is rarely random. Clinicians frequently prescribe therapies based on patient characteristics (\(X\)), such as baseline disease severity or age, which are also directly linked to the clinical outcome (\(Y\)). This non-random assignment leads to Selection Bias (Confounding by Indication).
For instance, in oncology appraisals, a newly launched therapy is often reserved for patients who have failed multiple lines of prior therapy or have a poor performance status. If we directly compare the survival outcomes of patients receiving the new therapy against those on standard of care (SOC), the naive treatment effect will be severely biased downward. The new drug’s efficacy is masked by the fact that its recipient group had a much worse prognosis at baseline.

1.1 The Dimension Reduction Problem
To estimate a causal effect, we must control for the baseline covariates \(X\). If we attempt to match patients on multiple characteristics simultaneously (e.g., matching a treated patient with a control patient who has the exact same age, gender, biomarkers, and comorbidities), we quickly encounter the Curse of Dimensionality. As the number of covariates increases, the probability of finding an exact match in a finite sample approaches zero.
Propensity Score Methods solve this problem by collapsing the high-dimensional covariate space \(X\) into a one-dimensional summary metric: the Propensity Score (PS).

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
text:
2 Propensity Score Matching (PSM)

2.1 Core Logic & The S-Curve
The Propensity Score \(e(X)\) is defined as the conditional probability of receiving treatment given a vector of observed baseline covariates \(X\): \[e(X) = P(D = 1 \mid X)\]
Because probability is bounded between 0 (never treated) and 1 (always treated), a standard linear model (\(D = \beta X + \epsilon\)) is inappropriate as it can predict values outside this range. We therefore model the propensity score using a Logistic Regression (Logit) model: \[P(D=1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\] where \(z\) is the linear combination of the confounders: \[z = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_k X_k\]
Taking the natural logarithm of the odds (the Logit transformation) yields a linear representation: \[\ln\left(\frac{P(D=1 \mid X)}{1 - P(D=1 \mid X)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \dots + \beta_k X_k\]
By matching treated and control patients who have the same (or very similar) propensity scores, we neutralize the baseline covariates. Within a matched block, the distribution of covariates \(X\) is balanced between the treated and control groups, effectively simulating a Pseudo-Randomized Controlled Trial (Pseudo-RCT).


2.2 Matching Constraints & ATT Estimation

Caliper Width: When matching, we do not require exact propensity score matches. Instead, we specify a tolerance zone or caliper (typically \(0.2\) times the standard deviation of the logit of the propensity score). If a treated patient’s propensity score is \(0.65\), we only match them with a control patient whose score falls within the caliper range.
Common Support: Propensity score matching is only valid within the region of Common Support—the overlap in propensity score distributions between the treated and control groups. Patients lying outside this overlap (e.g., treated patients with extremely high propensity scores who have no comparable controls) must be discarded.
ATT Estimation: By starting with the treated patients and searching for control twins, PSM estimates the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) by default: \[ATT = E[Y^{(1)} - Y^{(0)} \mid D=1]\] In HTA appraisals, the ATT is highly relevant because payers want to know the therapeutic benefit specifically for the patient population that clinicians would target in real-world practice.

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
text:
3 Inverse Probability Treatment Weighting (IPTW)
While PSM discards unmatched patients, Inverse Probability Treatment Weighting (IPTW) retains the entire sample. It balances the groups by assigning each patient a weight (\(W\)) inversely proportional to the probability of receiving the treatment they actually received.

3.1 The Weighting Mechanism
The Horvitz-Thompson weights for estimating the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) across the entire population are defined as: \[W_i = \frac{D_i}{e(X_i)} + \frac{1 - D_i}{1 - e(X_i)}\]

Treated Patients (\(D_i = 1\)): Weighted by \(1/e(X_i)\). A treated patient with a low probability of treatment (rare) represents a larger, unobserved segment of similar patients and is weighted up.
Control Patients (\(D_i = 0\)): Weighted by \(1/(1-e(X_i))\).

This weighting process creates a Weighted Pseudo-Population where the baseline covariate distributions in both groups are identical, allowing us to estimate the ATE: \[ATE = E[Y^{(1)} - Y^{(0)}]\]


3.2 Weighted Least Squares (WLS) Algebra
In practice, the treatment effect is estimated using Weighted Least Squares (WLS). The objective is to minimize the weighted sum of squared residuals: \[\sum_{i=1}^n W_i (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2\]
In matrix notation, the normal equation for the regression coefficients is modified from the standard OLS \((X'X)^{-1}X'Y\) to: \[\hat{\beta}_{WLS} = (X'WX)^{-1}X'WY\]


3.3 Statistical Inference & Robust Standard Errors
A common misconception in observational studies is that the standard error of the weighted treatment effect can be computed by treating the weighted groups as two independent samples (e.g., using the simple addition of independent normal variances: \(SE = \sqrt{Var(\bar{Y}_1) + Var(\bar{Y}_0)}\)). In HTA practice, this naive approach is strictly rejected for three reasons:

Non-Independence: The treated and control groups are not independent samples drawn from separate populations. They are subgroups of the same observational cohort, meaning their baseline covariates and potential outcomes share a joint distribution.
Variance Inflation: Weighting introduces unequal weights (\(W_i \neq 1\)), which violates the homoscedasticity assumption of standard OLS. Failing to adjust for this leads to severely underestimated standard errors and inflated Type I error rates.
Estimation Uncertainty of Propensity Scores: The propensity scores \(e(X)\) are not true population parameters; they are estimated from the data. This estimation process introduces auxiliary uncertainty that must propagate into the final treatment effect variance.







NoteTechnical Math: M-Estimation & The Sandwich Variance Estimator





To obtain asymptotically correct standard errors, modern causal inference relies on the M-Estimation (Empirical Sandwich Covariance) framework. We stack the estimating equations for the treatment assignment model (propensity score) and the outcome regression model together as a joint system:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \Psi_i(\theta) = 0\]
where \(\theta = [\beta, \alpha]^T\) is the combined parameter vector containing the propensity model coefficients \(\beta\) (logistic regression) and the outcome model coefficients \(\alpha\) (WLS regression).
The stacked estimating equations \(\Psi_i(\theta)\) for individual \(i\) are: \[\Psi_i(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix}
X_i \left( D_i - \text{logit}^{-1}(X_i \beta) \right) \\
W_i(\beta) \cdot Z_i \left( Y_i - Z_i \alpha \right)
\end{bmatrix}\]
where \(Z_i = [1, D_i]^T\) is the covariate vector of the outcome model, and \(W_i(\beta) = \frac{D_i}{\text{logit}^{-1}(X_i \beta)} + \frac{1 - D_i}{1 - \text{logit}^{-1}(X_i \beta)}\) are the estimated weights.
By Taylor expansion of the joint estimating equations, the asymptotic variance-covariance matrix of \(\hat{\theta}\) is given by the Sandwich Formula:
\[V(\hat{\theta}) = A(\hat{\theta})^{-1} B(\hat{\theta}) A(\hat{\theta})^{-T}\]

The “Bread” Matrix \(A(\hat{\theta})\): The expected Jacobian matrix of the estimating equations: \[A(\hat{\theta}) = - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial \Psi_i(\theta)}{\partial \theta}\] The off-diagonal blocks of \(A(\hat{\theta})\) capture the dependence of the outcome estimating equations on the propensity score parameters \(\beta\). This explicitly accounts for the uncertainty introduced by estimating the weights.
The “Meat” Matrix \(B(\hat{\theta})\): The empirical variance of the estimating equations: \[B(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \Psi_i(\theta) \Psi_i(\theta)^T\] which allows for heteroscedasticity and clustering.

Once the robust variance of the treatment effect coefficient \(\hat{\alpha}_1\) (the ATE estimate) is extracted from the diagonal of \(V(\hat{\theta})\) as \(SE_{\text{robust}}\), the 95% Confidence Interval is constructed using the standard Wald formulation: \[CI_{95\%} = \hat{\alpha}_1 \pm 1.96 \cdot SE_{\text{robust}}\]
This is the exact methodology executed by lm_weightit under the hood, ensuring that the confidence intervals presented in the portfolio are methodologically rigorous and defensible.





3.4 Effective Sample Size (ESS)
Because weighting inflates the influence of certain individuals, the statistical precision of the weighted sample is lower than the nominal sample size. We quantify this information loss using Kish’s Effective Sample Size (ESS): \[ESS = \frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^n W_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n W_i^2}\]
If all weights are uniform (\(W_i=1\)), the ESS equals the actual sample size \(N\). If a few patients have extremely large weights, the denominator increases, and the ESS collapses, signaling that the treatment effect estimate is dominated by a tiny fraction of the population.

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
text:
4 Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW)
Augmented IPTW (AIPW) is a Doubly Robust (DR) estimator that resolves the primary vulnerability of both standard regression models and propensity score weighting. It achieves this by combining an outcome regression (OR) model with a treatment assignment (propensity score) model.

4.1 The “Belt and Suspenders” Philosophy
To construct the AIPW estimator, we fit two distinct models on the observed data:

The Treatment Model (Propensity Score Model, \(g(X)\)): Predicts the probability of receiving treatment (\(D\)) given baseline covariates (\(X\)). Concretely, using a logistic model: \[g(X) = P(D = 1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{ECOG})}}\]
The Outcome Model (\(m_d(X)\)): Predicts the clinical outcome (\(Y\)) given the treatment assignment (\(D\)) and baseline covariates (\(X\)).

What is the Outcome \(Y\)? In our simulated oncology scenario, \(Y\) is the 1-year survival indicator—a binary clinical endpoint (\(Y_i = 1\) if patient \(i\) is alive at 1 year, and \(Y_i = 0\) if deceased).
Concretely, what does the Outcome Model look like? Because \(Y\) is binary, we model the conditional expectation \(E[Y \mid D, X] = P(Y = 1 \mid D, X)\) using a logistic regression model: \[E[Y \mid D, X] = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 D + \alpha_2 \cdot \text{Age} + \alpha_3 \cdot \text{ECOG})}}\] where \(\alpha_1\) is the conditional log-odds ratio associated with treatment, and \(\alpha_2, \alpha_3\) adjust for baseline confounding.
How are the counterfactual predictions generated? Once the outcome model is fitted and its coefficients \(\hat{\alpha}\) are estimated, we generate two predicted values for every patient \(i\) in the sample by plugging in the treatment indicator (\(d = 1\) and \(d = 0\)) while keeping their baseline covariates (\(X_i\)) unchanged:

Predicted survival under treatment (\(d = 1\)): \[m_1(X_i) = \hat{P}(Y_i^{(1)} = 1 \mid X_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\hat{\alpha}_0 + \hat{\alpha}_1 \cdot 1 + \hat{\alpha}_2 \cdot \text{Age}_i + \hat{\alpha}_3 \cdot \text{ECOG}_i)}}\]
Predicted survival under control (\(d = 0\)): \[m_0(X_i) = \hat{P}(Y_i^{(0)} = 1 \mid X_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\hat{\alpha}_0 + \hat{\alpha}_1 \cdot 0 + \hat{\alpha}_2 \cdot \text{Age}_i + \hat{\alpha}_3 \cdot \text{ECOG}_i)}}\]



The AIPW estimator aggregates these predictions alongside the propensity score weights. The counterfactual mean under treatment (\(d = 1\)) is: \[\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ m_1(X_i) + \frac{D_i (Y_i - m_1(X_i))}{g(X_i)} \right]\]
Similarly, the counterfactual mean under control (\(d = 0\)) is: \[\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(0)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ m_0(X_i) + \frac{(1 - D_i) (Y_i - m_0(X_i))}{1 - g(X_i)} \right]\]
The doubly robust Average Treatment Effect (ATE) estimator is the difference: \[\hat{ATE}_{AIPW} = \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} - \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(0)}\]



4.2 Structural Anatomy of the Estimator
Let’s dissect the mathematical structure of \(\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)}\) to understand its components:
\[\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ \underbrace{m_1(X_i)}_{\text{Component A}} + \underbrace{\frac{D_i (Y_i - m_1(X_i))}{g(X_i)}}_{\text{Component B}} \Big]\]

Component A: Base Prediction (G-Computation) This represents the outcome predicted by the outcome model for patient \(i\) under the treatment condition, based on their baseline covariates. If the outcome model is correct, the average of this term across the entire sample is an unbiased estimate of the counterfactual mean.
Component B: Weighted Residual Correction (Bias Adjuster) This term scales the residual error \((Y_i - m_1(X_i))\) of the outcome model for treated patients using the inverse of the propensity score.

If the outcome model is incorrect, this residual is non-zero. The term captures this systematic prediction bias and adds it back to Component A, correcting the estimate.
If the propensity score model is correct, the expectation of this correction term exactly offsets any bias in the outcome model.
Additionally, this component acts as a control variate (a variance reduction technique). By centering the outcome \(Y_i\) around its conditional mean \(m_1(X_i)\), we minimize the variance inflation caused by extreme weights in standard IPTW.





4.3 Step-by-Step Proof of Double Robustness
AIPW is doubly robust because it yields an unbiased estimate if either the propensity score model \(g(X)\) or the outcome regression model \(m_1(X)\) is correctly specified.






NoteStep-by-Step Mathematical Proof of Double Robustness





We prove this using the Law of Iterated Expectations (LIE): \[E[Z] = E_X \big[ E[Z \mid X] \big]\]

4.3.1 Assumptions Required:

Consistency: \(Y_i = D_i Y_i^{(1)} + (1 - D_i) Y_i^{(0)}\). For treated patients (\(D_i = 1\)), the observed outcome is the potential outcome under treatment: \(Y_i = Y_i^{(1)}\).
Conditional Independence (Unconfoundedness): Causal potential outcomes are independent of treatment assignment given baseline covariates: \(Y^{(1)}, Y^{(0)} \perp D \mid X\).

Let \(\hat{g}(X)\) and \(\hat{m}_1(X)\) be our estimated models. The expectation of the AIPW estimator under treatment is: \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \right] = E_X \left[ E\left[ \hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i))}{\hat{g}(X_i)} \;\middle|\; X_i \right] \right]\]



4.3.2 Case 1: Propensity Model is Correct (\(\hat{g}(X) = g(X)\)), Outcome Model is Misspecified (\(\hat{m}_1(X) \neq m_1(X)\))
If the propensity score model is correct, we have \(E[D_i \mid X_i] = \hat{g}(X_i) = g(X_i)\).
Let’s evaluate the conditional expectation of the estimator’s terms given \(X_i\): \[E\left[ \hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i))}{\hat{g}(X_i)} \;\middle|\; X_i \right] = \hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right]}{g(X_i)}\]
Using consistency (\(D_i Y_i = D_i Y_i^{(1)}\)) and conditioning: \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i Y_i^{(1)} - D_i \hat{m}_1(X_i) \mid X_i \right]\]
By the Conditional Independence assumption (\(Y^{(1)} \perp D \mid X\)): \[E\left[ D_i Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i \mid X_i \right] \cdot E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = g(X_i) E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\]
Similarly, since \(\hat{m}_1(X_i)\) is a deterministic function of \(X_i\): \[E\left[ D_i \hat{m}_1(X_i) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i \mid X_i \right] \cdot \hat{m}_1(X_i) = g(X_i) \hat{m}_1(X_i)\]
Substitute these expectations back into the numerator: \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right] = g(X_i) E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - g(X_i) \hat{m}_1(X_i) = g(X_i) \left( E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - \hat{m}_1(X_i) \right)\]
Now substitute this back into the estimator: \[\hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{g(X_i) \left( E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - \hat{m}_1(X_i) \right)}{g(X_i)} = \hat{m}_1(X_i) + E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - \hat{m}_1(X_i) = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\]
Taking the outer expectation over the covariate distribution \(X\): \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \right] = E_X \Big[ E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] \Big] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \right]\]
Result: The estimate is unbiased. The incorrect predictions of the outcome model (\(\hat{m}_1(X_i)\)) are algebraically canceled out by the weighted residual term.



4.3.3 Case 2: Outcome Model is Correct (\(\hat{m}_1(X) = m_1(X)\)), Propensity Model is Misspecified (\(\hat{g}(X) \neq g(X)\))
If the outcome model is correctly specified, we have \(\hat{m}_1(X_i) = m_1(X_i) = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\).
Let’s evaluate the conditional expectation of the residual correction term numerator given \(X_i\): \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \mid X_i \right]\]
Conditioning further on treatment assignment \(D_i\) using the Law of Iterated Expectations: \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \mid X_i \right] = E_{D \mid X} \left[ E\left[ D_i (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \;\middle|\; X_i, D_i \right] \right]\]
Since \(D_i\) is binary, this expectation only has a non-zero value when \(D_i = 1\): \[P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i) \cdot E\left[ 1 \cdot (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \;\middle|\; X_i, D_i = 1 \right]\]
By the Conditional Independence assumption (\(Y^{(1)} \perp D \mid X\)): \[E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] \;\middle|\; X_i, D_i = 1 \right] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = 0\]
Since the conditional expectation of the numerator is \(0\): \[E\left[ \frac{D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i))}{\hat{g}(X_i)} \;\middle|\; X_i \right] = 0\]
Therefore, the expectation of the estimator simplifies to: \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ \hat{m}_1(X_i) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\]
Taking the outer expectation over the covariate distribution \(X\): \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \right] = E_X \Big[ E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] \Big] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \right]\]
Result: The estimate is unbiased. Since the outcome model is correct, the expected residual error is \(0\). The incorrect propensity weights (\(\hat{g}(X_i)\)) are multiplied by zero and fail to introduce any bias.







4.4 Comparison: Why AIPW is Preferred in HTA








Feature
Standard IPTW
AIPW (Augmented IPTW)




Estimator Type
Single-robust (Propensity score only)
Doubly-robust (Propensity score + Outcome regression)

Severe bias if PS model is wrong
Unbiased if either model is correct


Variance (Efficiency)

Low variance (uses outcome predictions as control variates)

Moderately accepted; heavily criticized for extreme weights
Highly preferred; provides minimum variance bounds (semiparametric efficiency)

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
text:
5 R Implementation Pipeline
This pipeline simulates a real-world dataset (\(N=500\)) with a severe confounding by indication trap: high-risk, elderly patients with poor performance status (ECOG=1) are preferentially prescribed the new therapy (Drug X), masking its true survival benefit.


R Code
library(WeightIt)
library(cobalt)
library(survey)
library(AIPW)
library(SuperLearner)

set.seed(2026)
n <- 500

# 1. Simulate Confounders
age <- rnorm(n, mean = 65, sd = 10)
ecog <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4) # 1 = Poor performance status

# 2. Simulate Treatment Assignment (Confounding by Indication)
# Elderly and severe patients are more likely to receive Drug X (treatment = 1)
ps_true <- plogis(-2 + 0.05 * age + 1.2 * ecog)
treatment <- rbinom(n, 1, ps_true)

# 3. Simulate Survival Outcome (1-Year Survival)
# The treatment coefficient is +0.8 on the log-odds (logit) scale.
# Across the covariate distribution, this corresponds to a true marginal Risk Difference (ATE) of +15.5%.
y_prob <- plogis(1 - 0.03 * age - 1.0 * ecog + 0.8 * treatment)
survival_1yr <- rbinom(n, 1, y_prob)

df <- data.frame(age, ecog, treatment, survival_1yr)

# Calculate Naive (Unadjusted) Estimate
naive_treated <- mean(df$survival_1yr[df$treatment == 1])
naive_control <- mean(df$survival_1yr[df$treatment == 0])
naive_ate <- naive_treated - naive_control








NoteMethodological Note: Log-Odds vs. Risk Difference (ATE)



In observational binary outcome simulations (like 1-year survival), the treatment effect is defined on the log-odds ratio scale (+0.8 in the regression formula) rather than as a direct additive percentage. Because the logit function is non-linear, a log-odds coefficient of 0.8 does not translate to a constant risk difference for all patients.
To determine the true marginal Risk Difference (ATE) for the population, we calculate the difference in expected probabilities under treatment and control states for each individual, and then average them over the baseline covariate distribution: \[ATE = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[ \text{logit}^{-1}(1 - 0.03 \cdot \text{Age}_i - 1.0 \cdot \text{ECOG}_i + 0.8) - \text{logit}^{-1}(1 - 0.03 \cdot \text{Age}_i - 1.0 \cdot \text{ECOG}_i) \right]\]
For this simulated cohort, the true population ATE is exactly +15.5%.



5.1 Baseline Diagnostics (Original Data)
Without adjustment, patients receiving Drug X are significantly older and have worse ECOG scores, creating a naive survival comparison that underestimates the treatment effect:


R Code
# Create baseline characteristics table

n_ctl <- sum(df$treatment == 0)

mean_age_trt <- mean(df$age[df$treatment == 1])
sd_age_trt <- sd(df$age[df$treatment == 1])
mean_age_ctl <- mean(df$age[df$treatment == 0])

ecog1_trt <- sum(df$ecog[df$treatment == 1] == 1)
ecog1_ctl <- sum(df$ecog[df$treatment == 0] == 1)

surv_trt <- sum(df$survival_1yr[df$treatment == 1] == 1)

baseline_tbl <- data.frame(

    "Sample Size, N (%)",

  ),

We apply WeightIt to calculate propensity weights and evaluate baseline balance.

# Extract Effective Sample Size (ESS)

A standardized mean difference (SMD) below \(0.1\) indicates that the baseline confounding has been successfully balanced between groups.


R Code
love.plot(W,
          thresholds = c(m = 0.1),
          binary = "std",
          abs = TRUE,

          sample.names = c("Original", "Weighted"))











5.4 Treatment Effect Estimation (IPTW & AIPW)
We fit a weighted regression model using lm_weightit to calculate the IPTW estimate with robust standard errors, followed by doubly robust estimation via AIPW.


R Code
# 1. IPTW Weighted Linear Regression
fit_iptw <- lm_weightit(survival_1yr ~ treatment,
                        data = df,
                        weightit = W)

iptw_summary <- summary(fit_iptw)
iptw_est <- iptw_summary$coefficients["treatment", "Estimate"]
iptw_se <- iptw_summary$coefficients["treatment", "Std. Error"]

# Extract and format IPTW regression results for display
iptw_coefs <- iptw_summary$coefficients
iptw_cis <- confint(fit_iptw)

iptw_tbl <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Intercept (Control Survival)", "Treatment Effect (ATE)"),
  Estimate = round(iptw_coefs[, "Estimate"], 4),
  "Std. Error" = round(iptw_coefs[, "Std. Error"], 4),
  "z value" = round(iptw_coefs[, "z value"], 2),
  "p-value" = format.pval(iptw_coefs[, "Pr(>|z|)"], eps = 0.001, digits = 3),
  "95% LCL" = round(iptw_cis[, 1], 4),
  "95% UCL" = round(iptw_cis[, 2], 4),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
)

# 2. AIPW Estimation
sl_lib_aipw <- c("SL.glm", "SL.mean")

aipw_obj <- AIPW$new(
  Y = df$survival_1yr,
  A = df$treatment,
  W = df[, c("age", "ecog")],
  Q.SL.library = sl_lib_aipw,
  g.SL.library = sl_lib_aipw
)

# Run double robust estimation and suppress console messages/output
suppressMessages(aipw_obj$fit())
invisible(capture.output(aipw_obj$summary()))


# Extract and format AIPW results
aipw_res <- as.data.frame(aipw_obj$result)
aipw_est <- aipw_res["Risk Difference", "Estimate"]
aipw_se <- aipw_res["Risk Difference", "SE"]

# Create a clean data frame for AIPW outputs
aipw_tbl <- data.frame(
  Parameter = row.names(aipw_res),
  Estimate = round(aipw_res$Estimate, 4),
  "Std. Error" = round(aipw_res$SE, 4),
  "95% LCL" = round(aipw_res$`95% LCL`, 4),
  "95% UCL" = round(aipw_res$`95% UCL`, 4),
  "Sample Size (N)" = as.integer(aipw_res$N),
  check.names = FALSE
)

NoteMethodological Note: Epidemiological “Risk” Terminology



In biostatistics and epidemiological software packages (such as AIPW), the term “Risk” is the standard mathematical synonym for the probability of the outcome occurring, regardless of whether the event is clinically positive (e.g., survival) or negative (e.g., mortality).
In this simulation:

Risk of Exposure refers to the predicted probability of survival under the treated state (Drug X): \(P(Y^{(1)} = 1)\).
Risk of Control refers to the predicted probability of survival under the untreated state (Standard of Care): \(P(Y^{(0)} = 1)\).
Risk Difference is the absolute difference in survival probabilities, representing the marginal Average Treatment Effect (ATE): \(P(Y^{(1)} = 1) - P(Y^{(0)} = 1)\).
Risk Ratio is the Relative Risk (RR) of survival under treatment vs. control: \(P(Y^{(1)} = 1) / P(Y^{(0)} = 1)\).

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
text:
6 Advanced HTA Considerations & EAG Defense

6.1 Boundary Explosions (\(PS \to 0\) or \(1\))
In observational datasets, physician prescribing preferences can result in near-deterministic treatment assignments for certain patient subgroups. This leads to propensity scores that approach \(0\) or \(1\).

The Hazard: For a treated patient with \(PS = 0.01\), the weight is \(W = 100\). This single outlier’s outcome is multiplied a hundredfold in the pseudo-population, destabilizing the clinical outcome model.
The Defense:

Stabilized Weights: We scale the weights by the marginal probability of treatment \(P(D)\) in the sample: \[W_{stabilized} = D \cdot \frac{P(D=1)}{PS} + (1 - D) \cdot \frac{P(D=0)}{1 - PS}\] This scales down extreme weights globally.
Weight Trimming: If weights remain extreme after stabilization, we apply asymmetric trimming (e.g., trimming the top and bottom 1% of the weight distribution). While trimming introduces a small amount of bias by changing the target population, it significantly reduces variance and stabilizes survival extrapolations, which is generally accepted by NICE EAGs.




6.2 Methodological Trade-offs









Characteristic
Propensity Score Matching (PSM)
Inverse Probability Weighting (IPTW)
Augmented IPTW (AIPW)




Sample Retention
Discards unmatched patients (sample loss)
Retains entire sample via weighting
Retains entire sample via weighting


Causal Parameter
ATT (Effect on the Treated)
ATE (Effect on the Population)
ATE (Effect on the Population)


Sensitivity to Model Misspecification
High (Relies entirely on PS model correctness)
High (Relies entirely on PS model correctness)
Low (Doubly Robust: unbiased if either PS or outcome model is correct)


Efficiency (Variance)
Lower (due to sample size reduction)
Higher (uses all data, but can be skewed by extreme weights)

Low (extreme patients excluded naturally)
High (due to extreme weights from poor overlap)
Moderate (stabilized by outcome model residuals)

title: HEOR Core Metrics: OR vs HR Intuition Guide
text:
In health technology assessment (HTA) submissions, clinical evidence is summarized using various relative treatment effects. The choice of these metrics is not arbitrary; it dictates how clinical efficacy is translated into survival curves, state occupancy traces, and ultimately cost-effectiveness results (QALYs and ICERs).
Two of the most frequently used—and often misunderstood—relative metrics are:

Odds Ratio (OR): A static, cross-sectional measure comparing the odds of an event.
Hazard Ratio (HR): A dynamic, time-to-event measure comparing the instantaneous rate of event occurrence.


This guide provides the mathematical derivations, statistical properties, R implementations, and strategic HTA implications of these two core metrics.

title: HEOR Core Metrics: OR vs HR Intuition Guide
section: 2 Survival Functions Derivation: From Hazard to Survival
text:
2 Survival Functions Derivation: From Hazard to Survival
To understand the Hazard Ratio, we must first understand the relationship between the instantaneous Hazard Rate \(h(t)\), Cumulative Hazard \(H(t)\), and the Survival Function \(S(t)\).

2.1 Mathematical Definitions
Let \(T \ge 0\) represent the random variable for time-to-event.1
1 Denotes survival time, measuring the duration from trial baseline to the event of interest. In parametric survival modeling, this random variable \(T\) is assumed to follow distributions like the Weibull, Log-Normal, or Gompertz.
Survival Function \(S(t)\): The probability of surviving (i.e., not experiencing the event) beyond time \(t\): \[S(t) = P(T > t)\]
Cumulative Distribution Function \(F(t)\): The probability of experiencing the event by time \(t\): \[F(t) = P(T \le t) = 1 - S(t)\]
Probability Density Function \(f(t)\): The rate of event occurrence per unit of time: \[f(t) = \frac{d}{dt}F(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(1 - S(t)) = -S'(t)\]
Hazard Rate \(h(t)\): The instantaneous failure rate at time \(t\), conditional on survival up to \(t\): \[h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{P(t \le T < t + \Delta t \mid T \ge t)}{\Delta t} = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)}\]



2.2 Step-by-Step Derivation of \(S(t)\)

Step 1: Express \(h(t)\) in terms of \(S(t)\) and its derivative
Substitute \(f(t) = -S'(t)\) into the definition of \(h(t)\): \[h(t) = \frac{-S'(t)}{S(t)}\]


Step 2: Recognize the derivative of the natural logarithm
By the chain rule: \[\frac{d}{dt}\ln(S(t)) = \frac{S'(t)}{S(t)}\] Substituting this back into Step 1 yields: \[h(t) = -\frac{d}{dt}\ln(S(t))\]


Step 3: Integrate both sides
Integrate both sides from \(0\) to \(t\): \[\int_0^t h(u) du = \int_0^t -\frac{d}{du}\ln(S(u)) du\] The left side is defined as the Cumulative Hazard Function \(H(t)\): \[H(t) = \int_0^t h(u) du\] The right side can be evaluated using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \[\int_0^t -\frac{d}{du}\ln(S(u)) du = [-\ln(S(u))]_0^t = -\ln(S(t)) - (-\ln(S(0)))\]


Step 4: Apply boundary conditions
At time \(t=0\), the probability of survival is \(1\), so \(S(0) = 1\). Since \(\ln(1) = 0\): \[H(t) = -\ln(S(t))\]


Step 5: Solve for \(S(t)\)
Multiply by \(-1\) and take the exponential of both sides: \[S(t) = e^{-H(t)} = \exp\left(-\int_0^t h(u) du\right)\]

title: HEOR Core Metrics: OR vs HR Intuition Guide
section: 3 Odds Ratio (OR): The Static Endpoint Snapshot
text:
3 Odds Ratio (OR): The Static Endpoint Snapshot
The Odds Ratio evaluates the relative likelihood of a binary outcome. It is widely used in HTA for endpoints like Complete Response (CR) rates, Adverse Event (AE) rates, or any cross-sectional indicator.

3.1 Mathematical Formulation

Probability (\(p\)): The proportion of times an event occurs (\(p \in [0, 1]\)). In a time-to-event context, if we define the binary event as experiencing the outcome (e.g., progression or death) by a specific time \(t\), this probability \(p\) is equivalent to the Cumulative Distribution Function \(F(t) = 1 - S(t)\) defined in the previous section.
Odds: The ratio of the probability of the event occurring to the probability of it not occurring: \[\text{Odds} = \frac{p}{1 - p}\]
Odds Ratio (OR): The ratio of the odds of the event in the treatment group to the odds of the event in the control group: \[\text{OR} = \frac{\text{Odds}_{\text{T}}}{\text{Odds}_{\text{C}}} = \frac{p_{\text{T}} / (1 - p_{\text{T}})}{p_{\text{C}} / (1 - p_{\text{C}})}\]



3.2 Logit Link and Logistic Regression
In evidence synthesis (such as Bayesian Meta-Analysis), relative treatment effects are modeled on the log-odds scale using the logit link function: \[\text{logit}(p) = \ln\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X\] Under this model: \[\ln(\text{OR}) = \text{logit}(p_{\text{T}}) - \text{logit}(p_{\text{C}}) = \beta_1\] \[\text{OR} = e^{\beta_1}\]

Strategic Rationale in HTA

Symmetry: The log-odds scale maps probabilities from \([0, 1]\) to \((-\infty, +\infty)\), preventing out-of-bounds predictions.
Appraisal Defence: Under a logistic framework, the OR remains mathematically stable across different study baseline risk levels, unlike the Relative Risk (RR), which is structurally constrained by the baseline rate (e.g., if control \(p_{\text{C}} = 0.6\), RR cannot exceed \(1.67\), but OR has no such restriction).




3.3 R Implementation: Calculating OR via Logistic Regression
To ground the mathematical definition, we simulate a Phase III randomized controlled trial evaluating a binary landmark endpoint, such as the Complete Response (CR) rate at 24 weeks. The trial consists of N = 500 patients randomized 1:1, with an assumed true response probability of 40% in the Control arm (p_C = 0.40) and 55% in the active Treatment arm (p_T = 0.55). Below is the R implementation to simulate this cohort, fit the logistic regression model, and calculate the Odds Ratio.


Code
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# Generate synthetic binary response data (e.g., Complete Response)
set.seed(2)
n_patients <- 500
data_binary <- data.frame(
  Treatment = c(rep("Control", n_patients/2), rep("Drug A", n_patients/2))
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Control has ~40% CR rate; Drug A has ~55% CR rate
    CR_prob = ifelse(Treatment == "Control", 0.40, 0.55),
    CR_achieved = rbinom(n(), 1, CR_prob)
  )

# 1. Direct cross-tabulation
table_cr <- table(data_binary$Treatment, data_binary$CR_achieved)
colnames(table_cr) <- c("No CR", "CR")

# 2. Fit Logistic Regression
fit_logistic <- glm(CR_achieved ~ Treatment, data = data_binary, family = binomial)

# 3. Extract log-odds and convert to Odds Ratio
summary_coef <- summary(fit_logistic)$coefficients
log_or <- summary_coef["TreatmentDrug A", "Estimate"]
se_log_or <- summary_coef["TreatmentDrug A", "Std. Error"]

or_est <- exp(log_or)
or_ci_lower <- exp(log_or - 1.96 * se_log_or)
or_ci_upper <- exp(log_or + 1.96 * se_log_or)

true_or <- (0.55 / 0.45) / (0.40 / 0.60)
true_log_or <- log(true_or)

results_df <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Log-Odds (Beta)", "Odds Ratio (OR)"),
  `True Parameter` = c(round(true_log_or, 4), round(true_or, 3)),
  Estimate = c(round(log_or, 4), round(or_est, 3)),
  `Std. Error` = c(round(se_log_or, 4), "-"),
  `95% CI` = c(
    sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", log_or - 1.96 * se_log_or, log_or + 1.96 * se_log_or),
    sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", or_ci_lower, or_ci_upper)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

# 4. Display results as styled tables

title: HEOR Core Metrics: OR vs HR Intuition Guide
section: 4 Hazard Ratio (HR): The Dynamic Instantaneous Velocity
text:
4 Hazard Ratio (HR): The Dynamic Instantaneous Velocity
The Hazard Ratio is the standard relative metric for time-to-event outcomes, such as Overall Survival (OS) or Progression-Free Survival (PFS).
The Cox Proportional Hazards (PH) framework is a semi-parametric regression model widely used in survival analysis to relate the survival time of patients to one or more predictor variables. By modeling the hazard rate as a function of covariates without specifying the functional form of the baseline hazard, it offers a flexible and robust way to estimate relative treatment effects.

4.1 The Proportional Hazards (PH) Assumption
Under the Cox Proportional Hazards framework, the hazard for an individual with covariate vector \(X\) is: \[h(t \mid X) = h_0(t) e^{\beta X}\] Where \(h_0(t)\) is the baseline hazard function. The Hazard Ratio comparing treatment (\(X=1\)) to control (\(X=0\)) is: \[\text{HR}(t) = \frac{h(t \mid X=1)}{h(t \mid X=0)} = \frac{h_0(t) e^{\beta}}{h_0(t)} = e^{\beta}\] Since the baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\) cancels out, the HR is assumed to be constant over time.


4.2 Compatibility of Parametric Distributions with PH
In parametric survival analysis, only specific distributions are mathematically compatible with a constant Hazard Ratio:

Strictly PH-Compatible Distributions:

Exponential Distribution: Hazard rate \(h(t) = \lambda\) is constant. The ratio is \(\lambda_{\text{T}} / \lambda_{\text{C}}\), which is naturally constant.
Weibull Distribution: Hazard rate \(h(t) = \lambda \alpha t^{\alpha - 1}\). If we assume a shared shape parameter \(\alpha\) between arms, the hazard ratio is \(\lambda_{\text{T}} / \lambda_{\text{C}}\), which is constant.
Gompertz Distribution: Hazard rate \(h(t) = a e^{b t}\). If different arms share the growth rate \(b\), the HR is \(a_{\text{T}} / a_{\text{C}}\), which is constant.
Restricted Cubic Splines (on Log-Cumulative Hazard Scale / Royston-Parmar Model): These flexible parametric models use cubic splines (smooth polynomials joined at user-specified “knots”) to model the log-cumulative hazard function. If all spline parameters (representing the shape of the baseline log-cumulative hazard) are shared across treatment arms, and the treatment effect is modeled as a simple additive constant on the log-cumulative hazard scale (shifting only the intercept), the model enforces a constant Hazard Ratio. This allows for highly flexible baseline hazard shapes (e.g., bathtub or peaked shapes) while strictly maintaining the Proportional Hazards assumption.

Non-PH Distributions (Accelerated Failure Time / AFT):

Log-Normal, Log-Logistic, and Generalized Gamma: These assume that the treatment multiplies survival time (time acceleration/deceleration) rather than scaling the hazard. Under these distributions, the implied HR changes continuously over time, violating the Cox PH assumption.




4.3 R Implementation: Calculating HR via Cox Regression
Here is how to calculate and interpret the Hazard Ratio in R using synthetic survival data.


Code
library(survival)
library(knitr)

# Generate synthetic survival data
set.seed(18)
n_patients <- 200
data_survival <- data.frame(
  Treatment = c(rep(0, n_patients/2), rep(1, n_patients/2)) # 0: Control, 1: Drug A
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Generate Weibull-distributed survival times
    # Control: shape = 1.2, scale = 0.04 (median OS ~ 24 months)
    # Drug A: shape = 1.2, scale = 0.02 (median OS ~ 43 months; HR = 0.5)
    true_scale = ifelse(Treatment == 0, 0.04, 0.02),
    u = runif(n()),
    time = (-log(u) / true_scale)^(1/1.2),
    # Add random censoring before 60 months
    censor_time = runif(n(), 10, 80),
    observed_time = pmin(time, censor_time, 60),
    event = ifelse(time <= observed_time, 1, 0)
  )

# Fit Cox Proportional Hazards Model
fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(observed_time, event) ~ Treatment, data = data_survival)

# Extract and convert coefficients
summary_cox <- summary(fit_cox)
log_hr <- summary_cox$coefficients["Treatment", "coef"]
se_log_hr <- summary_cox$coefficients["Treatment", "se(coef)"]

hr_est <- exp(log_hr)
hr_ci_lower <- summary_cox$conf.int["Treatment", "lower .95"]
hr_ci_upper <- summary_cox$conf.int["Treatment", "upper .95"]

# True parameters: HR = 0.5, log(HR) = log(0.5) = -0.6931
true_hr <- 0.5
true_log_hr <- log(true_hr)

# Display results as a styled table
results_cox_df <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Log-Hazard (Beta)", "Hazard Ratio (HR)"),
  `True Parameter` = c(round(true_log_hr, 4), round(true_hr, 3)),
  Estimate = c(round(log_hr, 4), round(hr_est, 3)),
  `Std. Error` = c(round(se_log_hr, 4), "-"),
  `95% CI` = c(
    sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", log_hr - 1.96 * se_log_hr, log_hr + 1.96 * se_log_hr),
    sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", hr_ci_lower, hr_ci_upper)
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: HEOR Core Metrics: OR vs HR Intuition Guide
section: 5 Methodological Note: Key Differences & HTA Misconceptions
text:
5 Methodological Note: Key Differences & HTA Misconceptions
While both Odds Ratios (OR) and Hazard Ratios (HR) express relative treatment effects, they operate on different scales, represent different data structures, and are mathematically distinct.

5.1 Key Conceptual Differences

Static vs. Dynamic:

Odds Ratio (OR) is a static, cross-sectional measure at a specific landmark time point (e.g., Complete Response rate at 24 weeks). It ignores when events occurred or the velocity of their occurrence during the study.
Hazard Ratio (HR) is a dynamic, time-to-event measure that compares the instantaneous rate of event occurrence across the entire follow-up period.

Mathematical Definition:

OR represents the ratio of the odds of an event occurring (i.e., \(p / (1 - p)\)).
HR represents the ratio of the instantaneous hazard rates (i.e., \(h(t \mid X=1) / h(t \mid X=0)\)).




5.2 Common HTA Modeling Pitfalls

Avoid Direct Equivalency: A common error in indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) is treating an OR for a binary landmark survival endpoint (e.g., proportion of patients alive at 1 year) as a constant Hazard Ratio. Because the cumulative event rate changes over time, the relationship between the cumulative event OR and the underlying HR is non-linear and dynamic.
Survivor Bias: Applying an event-based OR (such as response or relapse rates) directly as a hazard multiplier in partitioned survival models or state transition models without accounting for baseline hazards introduces selection bias.
Effect Magnification: For common events (e.g., response rates around 50%), the OR is numerically more extreme (further from 1.0) than the Relative Risk (RR) or Hazard Ratio (HR), which can lead to overestimating treatment efficacy if misinterpreted.

title: HEOR Core Metrics: OR vs HR Intuition Guide
text:
6 Conclusion & Strategic Considerations
When drafting or auditing HTA submissions, ensure statistical coherence by following these guidelines:

Check scale consistency: Ensure all Weibull or spline parameters derived from trial analysis match the model cycle length (e.g., converting annual scale parameters to monthly).
Verify AFT distributions: If using Log-Normal or Log-Logistic curves, do not report a single, constant HR in the submission text, as it varies by design.
Avoid OR-to-HR conversions: Never use a constant conversion multiplier to convert binary ORs into time-to-event HRs.
Expose the ROI: Clearly demonstrate to the appraisal committee whether the drug’s value is driven by “entry” (Odds Ratio of response) or “durability” (Hazard Ratio of progression/relapse).

title: Multilevel Network Meta-Regression (ML-NMR)
text:
As demonstrated in Chapter 07, Simulated Treatment Comparison (STC) suffers from a mathematical fatal flaw when dealing with non-linear clinical endpoints (such as survival or binary outcomes): Ecological Bias. Because \(f(E[X]) \neq E[f(X)]\) for a non-linear link function \(f\), plugging aggregate means into a regression model will inevitably yield biased population-level predictions.
Multilevel Network Meta-Regression (ML-NMR) was specifically invented to solve this exact problem. It represents the state-of-the-art methodology for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons (PAIC) in Health Technology Assessment (HTA).
Instead of plugging in aggregate means, ML-NMR performs numerical integration over the target population’s covariate distribution (e.g., integrating over the age distribution). By projecting the individual-level non-linear relationship (from IPD) across the macro-level probability density function (PDF) of the AgD trial, ML-NMR successfully calculates \(E[f(X)]\) without ecological bias.
In this chapter, we will:

Simulate a realistic scenario with IPD and AgD (assuming the binary outcome \(y\) is Complete Remission (CR)).
Formulate the Joint Likelihood function.
Use numerical integration (Sobol sequences) to solve the ecological bias.
Run an ML-NMR using the industry-standard multinma package.
