title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 3 HTA Case Study: Drug X (METex14) Applied Case Study
text:
3 HTA Case Study: Drug X (METex14) Applied Case Study
To see how these principles apply to a real-world submission, we examine the case of Drug X, a precision oncology therapy for METex14-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).






NoteDeclaration: Simulated Proof-of-Methodology Case





This METex14 case is a self-generated proof-of-methodology example, not a real NICE submission, manufacturer dossier, or clinical claim about an identifiable medicine. Drug X, the sample sizes, data source details, and audit responses are simplified or fictionalized to demonstrate how target trial emulation, immortal time bias correction, and DataSAT-style reasoning can be documented in an HTA-facing RWE workflow.




3.1 Case Overview: The Drug X Conflict

The Innovation: Due to the rarity of the METex14 mutation and ethical constraints, only a Single-arm Trial (N=40) was conducted for Drug X.
The Challenge: A single-arm submission faces a high risk of rejection due to the lack of a randomized head-to-head comparison. Given the aggressive natural history of METex14 NSCLC, simple unadjusted benchmarking is insufficient for demonstrating comparative effectiveness.
The Strategy: We leverage the UK Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) database to construct an External Control Arm (ECA) of 200 patients, using the Target Trial Emulation (TTE) framework to satisfy NICE’s demand for rigorous causal inference.



3.2 Step 1: Data Suitability Audit (DataSAT)
According to Sections 3.1–3.3 of the NICE RWE Framework, we must prove the data is fit for purpose across three core dimensions:








Dimension
HTA Audit Response (HES Database)
NICE Framework Requirement




Provenance
Data sourced from NHS Digital with a clear audit trail from ICD-10 coding to the final analytical dataset.
Evaluate the origin and trustworthiness of data sources, methods of collection, and governance. (Section 3.1)


Quality
METex14 status confirmed via secondary linkage to SACT and genomic records; completeness checked for key covariates.
Assess the completeness and accuracy of eligibility criteria, exposures, and outcomes. (Section 3.2)


Relevance
HES covers 99% of NHS hospital activity, matching the SOC pathways in the UK.
Ensure findings generalise to the target population and clinical care pathways in the NHS. (Section 3.3)





3.3 Defining \(T_0\) (Zero-time Alignment)
To avoid Immortal Time Bias, we align \(T_0\) as the moment a patient meets all eligibility criteria AND is assigned to treatment, following the target trial approach described in Section 5.2 of the NICE RWE Framework. Basically, the index date and treatment strategy assignment must be defined without using future information. Treatment status observed after \(T_0\) cannot be used retrospectively to create baseline groups unless it is handled through a pre-specified grace-period strategy, such as cloning and censoring.

Why Immortal Time Bias is a “Statistical Killer”

Logic Paradox: In RWD studies, patients from diagnosis to actual treatment initiation (Drug X) face delays (e.g., 1 month). If follow-up begins at diagnosis, but grouping is based on whether they ever received treatment, the period before receiving the drug is immortal—if the patient died on Day 15, they would never have lived long enough to receive the drug, and would automatically be classified into the control group (since they are not “treated”).
Case Simulation:

Patient A: Diagnosed Jan 1, scheduled for Drug X, dies Jan 15 (unexposed). Classified as Control.
Patient B: Diagnosed Jan 1, initiates Drug X Feb 1, survives until June.
Result: The Drug X group artificially filters out those who die before treatment initiation, inflating the active group’s survival.

TTE Correction: The survival follow-up clock must be aligned to a clearly defined index date that is comparable across arms. If the estimand starts at diagnosis but treatment can begin during a grace period, the waiting time must not be retrospectively credited to the treated group; it should be handled using cloning-and-censoring, a time-varying exposure model, or a pre-specified landmark strategy.



The Control Arm \(T_0\)
Where does the control arm’s \(T_0\) start if they never receive the active treatment?

Synchronicity Principle: \(T_0\) is the moment the patient meets all clinical eligibility criteria (e.g., METex14 diagnosis + ECOG status).
Timeline Alignment:

Incorrect: Treated group starts at the “first recorded treatment start date”, while controls start at “diagnosis”. This gives the treated group an implicit survival benefit.
Correct TTE Approach: Both groups start follow-up at the exact date they meet all eligibility criteria (the clinical decision point, or clinical equipoise).




Handling the Grace Period
In RWD, a patient has a “window” of time (grace period) to initiate treatment (e.g., 30 days after diagnosis).

If a patient initiates treatment on Day 20, they contribute 20 days of “unexposed” person-time to the control group.
Using cloning, we create two clones at diagnosis. The “Control Clone” is followed until Day 20, where it is censored because the patient initiated treatment. The “Treated Clone” starts contributing treated time from Day 20 onwards.




3.4 Step 2: Cloning & Censoring Mechanics
To maintain ITT principles:

Anti-Future-Knowledge: We cannot look ahead to see what the patient did. We clone them at \(T_0\) into both paths.
Artificial Censoring: If the patient’s actual path deviates from a clone’s assigned arm, that clone is censored.
IPCW Weighting: Because censoring might be non-random, we estimate the probability of being censored at time \(t\) based on baseline covariates and apply Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights to the remaining patients, dynamically restoring the balance.

title: Propensity Score Methods: PSM, IPTW, and AIPW
text:
4 Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW)
Augmented IPTW (AIPW) is a Doubly Robust (DR) estimator that resolves the primary vulnerability of both standard regression models and propensity score weighting. It achieves this by combining an outcome regression (OR) model with a treatment assignment (propensity score) model.

4.1 The “Belt and Suspenders” Philosophy
To construct the AIPW estimator, we fit two distinct models on the observed data:

The Treatment Model (Propensity Score Model, \(g(X)\)): Predicts the probability of receiving treatment (\(D\)) given baseline covariates (\(X\)). Concretely, using a logistic model: \[g(X) = P(D = 1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{ECOG})}}\]
The Outcome Model (\(m_d(X)\)): Predicts the clinical outcome (\(Y\)) given the treatment assignment (\(D\)) and baseline covariates (\(X\)).

What is the Outcome \(Y\)? In our simulated oncology scenario, \(Y\) is the 1-year survival indicator—a binary clinical endpoint (\(Y_i = 1\) if patient \(i\) is alive at 1 year, and \(Y_i = 0\) if deceased).
Concretely, what does the Outcome Model look like? Because \(Y\) is binary, we model the conditional expectation \(E[Y \mid D, X] = P(Y = 1 \mid D, X)\) using a logistic regression model: \[E[Y \mid D, X] = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 D + \alpha_2 \cdot \text{Age} + \alpha_3 \cdot \text{ECOG})}}\] where \(\alpha_1\) is the conditional log-odds ratio associated with treatment, and \(\alpha_2, \alpha_3\) adjust for baseline confounding.
How are the counterfactual predictions generated? Once the outcome model is fitted and its coefficients \(\hat{\alpha}\) are estimated, we generate two predicted values for every patient \(i\) in the sample by plugging in the treatment indicator (\(d = 1\) and \(d = 0\)) while keeping their baseline covariates (\(X_i\)) unchanged:

Predicted survival under treatment (\(d = 1\)): \[m_1(X_i) = \hat{P}(Y_i^{(1)} = 1 \mid X_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\hat{\alpha}_0 + \hat{\alpha}_1 \cdot 1 + \hat{\alpha}_2 \cdot \text{Age}_i + \hat{\alpha}_3 \cdot \text{ECOG}_i)}}\]
Predicted survival under control (\(d = 0\)): \[m_0(X_i) = \hat{P}(Y_i^{(0)} = 1 \mid X_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\hat{\alpha}_0 + \hat{\alpha}_1 \cdot 0 + \hat{\alpha}_2 \cdot \text{Age}_i + \hat{\alpha}_3 \cdot \text{ECOG}_i)}}\]



The AIPW estimator aggregates these predictions alongside the propensity score weights. The counterfactual mean under treatment (\(d = 1\)) is: \[\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ m_1(X_i) + \frac{D_i (Y_i - m_1(X_i))}{g(X_i)} \right]\]
Similarly, the counterfactual mean under control (\(d = 0\)) is: \[\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(0)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ m_0(X_i) + \frac{(1 - D_i) (Y_i - m_0(X_i))}{1 - g(X_i)} \right]\]
The doubly robust Average Treatment Effect (ATE) estimator is the difference: \[\hat{ATE}_{AIPW} = \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} - \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(0)}\]



4.2 Structural Anatomy of the Estimator
Let’s dissect the mathematical structure of \(\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)}\) to understand its components:
\[\hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \Big[ \underbrace{m_1(X_i)}_{\text{Component A}} + \underbrace{\frac{D_i (Y_i - m_1(X_i))}{g(X_i)}}_{\text{Component B}} \Big]\]

Component A: Base Prediction (G-Computation) This represents the outcome predicted by the outcome model for patient \(i\) under the treatment condition, based on their baseline covariates. If the outcome model is correct, the average of this term across the entire sample is an unbiased estimate of the counterfactual mean.
Component B: Weighted Residual Correction (Bias Adjuster) This term scales the residual error \((Y_i - m_1(X_i))\) of the outcome model for treated patients using the inverse of the propensity score.

If the outcome model is incorrect, this residual is non-zero. The term captures this systematic prediction bias and adds it back to Component A, correcting the estimate.
If the propensity score model is correct, the expectation of this correction term exactly offsets any bias in the outcome model.
Additionally, this component acts as a control variate (a variance reduction technique). By centering the outcome \(Y_i\) around its conditional mean \(m_1(X_i)\), we minimize the variance inflation caused by extreme weights in standard IPTW.





4.3 Step-by-Step Proof of Double Robustness
AIPW is doubly robust because it yields an unbiased estimate if either the propensity score model \(g(X)\) or the outcome regression model \(m_1(X)\) is correctly specified.






NoteStep-by-Step Mathematical Proof of Double Robustness





We prove this using the Law of Iterated Expectations (LIE): \[E[Z] = E_X \big[ E[Z \mid X] \big]\]

4.3.1 Assumptions Required:

Consistency: \(Y_i = D_i Y_i^{(1)} + (1 - D_i) Y_i^{(0)}\). For treated patients (\(D_i = 1\)), the observed outcome is the potential outcome under treatment: \(Y_i = Y_i^{(1)}\).
Conditional Independence (Unconfoundedness): Causal potential outcomes are independent of treatment assignment given baseline covariates: \(Y^{(1)}, Y^{(0)} \perp D \mid X\).

Let \(\hat{g}(X)\) and \(\hat{m}_1(X)\) be our estimated models. The expectation of the AIPW estimator under treatment is: \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \right] = E_X \left[ E\left[ \hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i))}{\hat{g}(X_i)} \;\middle|\; X_i \right] \right]\]



4.3.2 Case 1: Propensity Model is Correct (\(\hat{g}(X) = g(X)\)), Outcome Model is Misspecified (\(\hat{m}_1(X) \neq m_1(X)\))
If the propensity score model is correct, we have \(E[D_i \mid X_i] = \hat{g}(X_i) = g(X_i)\).
Let’s evaluate the conditional expectation of the estimator’s terms given \(X_i\): \[E\left[ \hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i))}{\hat{g}(X_i)} \;\middle|\; X_i \right] = \hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right]}{g(X_i)}\]
Using consistency (\(D_i Y_i = D_i Y_i^{(1)}\)) and conditioning: \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i Y_i^{(1)} - D_i \hat{m}_1(X_i) \mid X_i \right]\]
By the Conditional Independence assumption (\(Y^{(1)} \perp D \mid X\)): \[E\left[ D_i Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i \mid X_i \right] \cdot E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = g(X_i) E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\]
Similarly, since \(\hat{m}_1(X_i)\) is a deterministic function of \(X_i\): \[E\left[ D_i \hat{m}_1(X_i) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i \mid X_i \right] \cdot \hat{m}_1(X_i) = g(X_i) \hat{m}_1(X_i)\]
Substitute these expectations back into the numerator: \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right] = g(X_i) E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - g(X_i) \hat{m}_1(X_i) = g(X_i) \left( E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - \hat{m}_1(X_i) \right)\]
Now substitute this back into the estimator: \[\hat{m}_1(X_i) + \frac{g(X_i) \left( E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - \hat{m}_1(X_i) \right)}{g(X_i)} = \hat{m}_1(X_i) + E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - \hat{m}_1(X_i) = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\]
Taking the outer expectation over the covariate distribution \(X\): \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \right] = E_X \Big[ E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] \Big] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \right]\]
Result: The estimate is unbiased. The incorrect predictions of the outcome model (\(\hat{m}_1(X_i)\)) are algebraically canceled out by the weighted residual term.



4.3.3 Case 2: Outcome Model is Correct (\(\hat{m}_1(X) = m_1(X)\)), Propensity Model is Misspecified (\(\hat{g}(X) \neq g(X)\))
If the outcome model is correctly specified, we have \(\hat{m}_1(X_i) = m_1(X_i) = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\).
Let’s evaluate the conditional expectation of the residual correction term numerator given \(X_i\): \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i)) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ D_i (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \mid X_i \right]\]
Conditioning further on treatment assignment \(D_i\) using the Law of Iterated Expectations: \[E\left[ D_i (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \mid X_i \right] = E_{D \mid X} \left[ E\left[ D_i (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \;\middle|\; X_i, D_i \right] \right]\]
Since \(D_i\) is binary, this expectation only has a non-zero value when \(D_i = 1\): \[P(D_i = 1 \mid X_i) \cdot E\left[ 1 \cdot (Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]) \;\middle|\; X_i, D_i = 1 \right]\]
By the Conditional Independence assumption (\(Y^{(1)} \perp D \mid X\)): \[E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] \;\middle|\; X_i, D_i = 1 \right] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] - E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = 0\]
Since the conditional expectation of the numerator is \(0\): \[E\left[ \frac{D_i (Y_i - \hat{m}_1(X_i))}{\hat{g}(X_i)} \;\middle|\; X_i \right] = 0\]
Therefore, the expectation of the estimator simplifies to: \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ \hat{m}_1(X_i) \mid X_i \right] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right]\]
Taking the outer expectation over the covariate distribution \(X\): \[E\left[ \hat{Y}_{AIPW}^{(1)} \right] = E_X \Big[ E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \mid X_i \right] \Big] = E\left[ Y_i^{(1)} \right]\]
Result: The estimate is unbiased. Since the outcome model is correct, the expected residual error is \(0\). The incorrect propensity weights (\(\hat{g}(X_i)\)) are multiplied by zero and fail to introduce any bias.







4.4 Comparison: Why AIPW is Preferred in HTA








Feature
Standard IPTW
AIPW (Augmented IPTW)




Estimator Type
Single-robust (Propensity score only)
Doubly-robust (Propensity score + Outcome regression)


Model Misspecification
Severe bias if PS model is wrong
Unbiased if either model is correct


Variance (Efficiency)
High variance due to extreme weights
Low variance (uses outcome predictions as control variates)


HTA / EAG Acceptance
Moderately accepted; heavily criticized for extreme weights
Highly preferred; provides minimum variance bounds (semiparametric efficiency)

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 7 Cloning, Censoring, and IPCW in Target Trial Emulation
text:
7 Cloning, Censoring, and IPCW in Target Trial Emulation
Time-dependent Cox models are useful for auditing whether delayed treatment initiation has created immortal time bias. However, when the target trial question is defined as a comparison of treatment strategies—for example, “initiate Drug X within 90 days of diagnosis” versus “do not initiate Drug X within 90 days”—a trial-emulation analysis often requires cloning, artificial censoring, and inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW). Here, the 90-day grace period is not a minor technical detail; it is part of the strategy definition itself and should be justified, audited, and tested in sensitivity analyses.3
3 Treatment status vs. treatment strategy: Imagine Drug X has strong biological efficacy once started, but testing and approval delays mean many patients die before receiving it. A time-dependent Cox model may show a large hazard reduction once patients are on Drug X. A cloning-censoring-IPCW analysis may still find limited benefit for the overall “start within 90 days” strategy unless treatment can actually be started fast enough. This is the difference between estimating an on-treatment effect and evaluating a baseline treatment-initiation strategy.
7.1 Why Artificial Censoring Creates Bias
In a cloned analysis, each patient is copied into every treatment strategy at \(T_0\):

One clone is assigned to the “initiate within grace period” strategy.
One clone is assigned to the “do not initiate within grace period” strategy.

Each clone is followed from the same \(T_0\). If the patient’s observed behavior becomes incompatible with a clone’s assigned strategy, that clone is artificially censored. For example, if the “no treatment” clone initiates Drug X on Day 20, that clone is censored on Day 20.
Artificial censoring can create selection bias because patients who violate a strategy are not random. For example, patients who start Drug X early may be younger, fitter, more urgent clinically, or treated in faster diagnostic pathways. After censoring the clones that violate their assigned strategy, the remaining uncensored clones may no longer represent the original eligible population. IPCW is used to reweight the remaining clones back toward that target population.
The direction of this bias depends on the clinical mechanism driving treatment timing. If more urgent patients start Drug X earlier, their “no initiation” clones are more likely to be censored, leaving a less urgent untreated-strategy group and potentially underestimating the benefit of Drug X. If earlier initiation is mainly driven by better access or fitter patients, the bias could move in the opposite direction.


7.2 IPCW Intuition
The “C” in IPCW stands for censoring. The core idea is to weight each remaining uncensored clone by the inverse of its probability of remaining uncensored:
\[
w_i(t) = \frac{1}{P(C_i(t)=0 \mid L_i)}
\]
where \(C_i(t)=0\) means clone \(i\) remains uncensored at time \(t\), and \(L_i\) represents baseline or time-updated covariate history.
The intuition is simple: if a type of patient is highly likely to be censored, but one such patient remains uncensored, that patient receives more weight because they represent similar patients who were censored.


7.3 Stabilized Weights
In practice, stabilized weights are often preferred because they reduce variance:
\[
SW_i(t) =
\frac{P(C_i(t)=0 \mid A_i)}
{P(C_i(t)=0 \mid A_i, L_i)}
\]
The denominator models censoring using strategy assignment and prognostic covariates. The numerator uses a simpler model, often including strategy assignment only. Extreme weights should be inspected and, if necessary, truncated using a pre-specified rule.


7.4 HTA Audit Checks
For an HTA-facing analysis, IPCW should not be presented as a black box. The submission should document:

the protocol rule that triggers artificial censoring;
the censoring model covariates and timing;
the distribution of stabilized weights;
any truncation threshold and its sensitivity analysis;
whether positivity is plausible across clinically relevant subgroups.



7.5 Applying Cloning-Censoring-IPCW
We now emulate a strategy-level target trial with a 90-day grace period:

Strategy 1: initiate Drug X within 90 days of diagnosis.
Strategy 0: do not initiate Drug X within 90 days of diagnosis.

Each patient is cloned into both strategies. A clone is artificially censored when the observed treatment path becomes incompatible with its assigned strategy.


R Code
grace_period <- 90

# 1. Clone each patient into both treatment strategies
df_clone <- rbind(
  transform(df, strategy = 1, strategy_label = "Initiate within 90 days"),
  transform(df, strategy = 0, strategy_label = "No initiation within 90 days")
)

# 2. Define artificial censoring rules
df_clone$artificial_censor_time <- Inf

# Strategy 1 violation: no treatment initiation by the end of the grace period
df_clone$artificial_censor_time[
  df_clone$strategy == 1 &
    df_clone$t_init > grace_period &
    df_clone$time > grace_period
] <- grace_period

# Strategy 0 violation: treatment initiation during the grace period
df_clone$artificial_censor_time[
  df_clone$strategy == 0 &
    df_clone$t_init <= grace_period &
    df_clone$t_init < df_clone$time
] <- df_clone$t_init[
  df_clone$strategy == 0 &
    df_clone$t_init <= grace_period &
    df_clone$t_init < df_clone$time
]

# 3. Observed follow-up under each assigned strategy
df_clone$obs_time <- pmin(df_clone$time, df_clone$artificial_censor_time)
df_clone$outcome_event <- as.integer(df_clone$event == 1 & df_clone$time <= df_clone$artificial_censor_time)
df_clone$artificial_censored <- as.integer(df_clone$artificial_censor_time < df_clone$time)
df_clone$uncensored <- 1 - df_clone$artificial_censored

  head(df_clone[, c("id", "strategy_label", "time", "event", "t_init", "obs_time", "outcome_event", "artificial_censored")], 8),
  caption = "Cloned Target Trial Dataset with Artificial Censoring Rules",

)

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 3 Applied Scenario: Zero-Time Alignment in an Oncology External Control Arm
text:
3 Applied Scenario: Zero-Time Alignment in an Oncology External Control Arm
To see how these principles apply in an HTA-facing RWE setting, consider Drug X, a precision oncology therapy for METex14-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).






NoteDeclaration: Simulated Proof-of-Methodology Scenario





This METex14 scenario is a self-generated proof-of-methodology example, not a real NICE submission, manufacturer dossier, or clinical claim about an identifiable medicine. Drug X, the sample sizes, data source details, and audit responses are simplified or fictionalized to demonstrate how target trial emulation, immortal time bias correction, and DataSAT-style reasoning can be documented in an HTA-facing RWE workflow.




3.1 Scenario Overview: The Drug X Challenge

The Innovation: Due to the rarity of the METex14 mutation and ethical constraints, only a Single-arm Trial (N=40) was conducted for Drug X.
The Challenge: A single-arm submission faces a high risk of rejection due to the lack of a randomized head-to-head comparison. Given the aggressive natural history of METex14 NSCLC, simple unadjusted benchmarking is insufficient for demonstrating comparative effectiveness.
The Strategy: We leverage the UK Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) database to construct an External Control Arm (ECA) of 200 patients, using the Target Trial Emulation (TTE) framework to satisfy NICE’s demand for rigorous causal inference.



3.2 Data Suitability Considerations (DataSAT)
According to Sections 3.1–3.3 of the NICE RWE Framework, we must prove the data is fit for purpose across three core dimensions:








Dimension
HTA Audit Response (HES Database)
NICE Framework Requirement




Provenance
Data sourced from NHS Digital with a clear audit trail from ICD-10 coding to the final analytical dataset.
Evaluate the origin and trustworthiness of data sources, methods of collection, and governance. (Section 3.1)


Quality
METex14 status confirmed via secondary linkage to SACT and genomic records; completeness checked for key covariates.
Assess the completeness and accuracy of eligibility criteria, exposures, and outcomes. (Section 3.2)


Relevance
HES covers 99% of NHS hospital activity, matching the SOC pathways in the UK.
Ensure findings generalise to the target population and clinical care pathways in the NHS. (Section 3.3)





3.3 Defining \(T_0\) (Zero-time Alignment)
To avoid Immortal Time Bias, we align \(T_0\) as the moment a patient meets all eligibility criteria AND is assigned to treatment, following the target trial approach described in Section 5.2 of the NICE RWE Framework. Basically, the index date and treatment strategy assignment must be defined without using future information. Treatment status observed after \(T_0\) cannot be used retrospectively to create baseline groups unless it is handled through a pre-specified grace-period strategy, such as cloning and censoring.

Why Immortal Time Bias is a “Statistical Killer”

Logic Paradox: In RWD studies, patients from diagnosis to actual treatment initiation (Drug X) face delays (e.g., 1 month). If follow-up begins at diagnosis, but grouping is based on whether they ever received treatment, the period before receiving the drug is immortal—if the patient died on Day 15, they would never have lived long enough to receive the drug, and would automatically be classified into the control group (since they are not “treated”).
Case Simulation:

Patient A: Diagnosed Jan 1, scheduled for Drug X, dies Jan 15 (unexposed). Classified as Control.
Patient B: Diagnosed Jan 1, initiates Drug X Feb 1, survives until June.
Result: The Drug X group artificially filters out those who die before treatment initiation, inflating the active group’s survival.

TTE Correction: The survival follow-up clock must be aligned to a clearly defined index date that is comparable across arms. If the causal question starts at diagnosis but treatment can begin during a grace period, the waiting time must not be retrospectively credited to the treated group; it should be handled using cloning-and-censoring, a time-varying exposure model, or a pre-specified landmark strategy.



The Control Arm \(T_0\)
Where does the control arm’s \(T_0\) start if they never receive the active treatment?

Synchronicity Principle: \(T_0\) is the moment the patient meets all clinical eligibility criteria (e.g., METex14 diagnosis + ECOG status).
Timeline Alignment:

Incorrect: Treated group starts at the “first recorded treatment start date”, while controls start at “diagnosis”. This gives the treated group an implicit survival benefit.
Correct TTE Approach: Both groups start follow-up at the exact date they meet all eligibility criteria (the clinical decision point, or clinical equipoise).




Handling the Grace Period
In RWD, a patient has a “window” of time (grace period) to initiate treatment (e.g., 30 days after diagnosis).

If a patient initiates treatment on Day 20, they contribute 20 days of “unexposed” person-time to the control group.
Using cloning, we create two clones at diagnosis. The “Control Clone” is followed until Day 20, where it is censored because the patient initiated treatment. The “Treated Clone” starts contributing treated time from Day 20 onwards.




3.4 Implication for Cloning & Censoring
To maintain ITT principles:

Anti-Future-Knowledge: We cannot look ahead to see what the patient did. We clone them at \(T_0\) into both paths.
Artificial Censoring: If the patient’s actual path deviates from a clone’s assigned arm, that clone is censored.
IPCW Weighting: Because censoring might be non-random, we estimate the probability of being censored at time \(t\) based on baseline covariates and apply Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights to the remaining patients, dynamically restoring the balance.

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 4 Simulated RWD Cohort: Delayed Treatment Initiation
text:
4 Simulated RWD Cohort: Delayed Treatment Initiation
To make the Drug X scenario concrete, we simulate a simplified RWD cohort with delayed treatment initiation. The simulated dataset is intentionally small enough to audit line by line, but it contains the core features that create immortal time bias:

baseline prognostic covariates: age and ECOG status;
treatment selection: older and sicker patients are more likely to receive Drug X;
treatment delay: treated patients have an observed treatment-initiation delay of 30 to 120 days; later, a 90-day grace period is used to define the target trial strategy;
time-to-event outcome: death or censoring during follow-up.

We simulate a true treatment Hazard Ratio of 0.70 (30% risk reduction). The purpose of the simulation is not to recreate a real METex14 dataset, but to create a controlled setting where the true parameter is known and different analytic choices can be compared.


R Code
library(survival)
library(EValue)
set.seed(42)
n <- 500

# 1. Simulate baseline confounders
age <- rnorm(n, mean = 60, sd = 10)
ecog <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)

# 2. Simulate treatment selection (confounding by indication)
# Sicker (ECOG=1) and older patients are more likely to receive Drug X
ps_prob <- plogis(-1.5 + 0.02 * age + 0.5 * ecog)
z_treatment <- rbinom(n, 1, ps_prob)

# Untreated patients are assigned Inf to indicate that treatment initiation never occurs
t_init <- ifelse(z_treatment == 1, runif(n, 30, 120), Inf)

# 3. Simulate survival times (true treatment HR = 0.70)
true_hr <- 0.70
lambda_base <- 0.001 * exp(0.02 * age + 0.5 * ecog)

u <- runif(n)
log_u <- -log(u)

pre_treatment_hazard <- lambda_base * t_init
event_before_treatment <- log_u <= pre_treatment_hazard

t_event <- ifelse(
  event_before_treatment,
  log_u / lambda_base,
  t_init + (log_u - pre_treatment_hazard) / (lambda_base * true_hr)
)

# Censoring between 150 and 730 days
t_censor <- runif(n, 150, 730)
time <- pmin(t_event, t_censor)
event <- as.integer(t_event <= t_censor)

df <- data.frame(id = 1:n, age, ecog, z_treatment, t_init, time, event)

# Future-informed treatment status: this is intentionally biased
df$ever_treated <- ifelse(df$t_init < df$time, 1, 0)
df$t_init_display <- ifelse(is.infinite(df$t_init), NA, df$t_init)

event_count <- sum(df$event)
event_pct <- mean(df$event) * 100

# Helper function used later to render Cox model summaries as kable tables
show_cox <- function(fit, caption) {
  sum_fit <- summary(fit)
  coefs <- sum_fit$coefficients
  cis <- sum_fit$conf.int
  se_col <- if ("robust se" %in% colnames(coefs)) "robust se" else "se(coef)"
  z_col <- if ("z" %in% colnames(coefs)) "z" else colnames(coefs)[4]
  tbl <- data.frame(
    Covariate = rownames(coefs),
    `Hazard Ratio` = round(coefs[, "exp(coef)"], 4),
    `Log HR (coef)` = round(coefs[, "coef"], 4),
    `Std Error` = round(coefs[, se_col], 4),
    `z-value` = round(coefs[, z_col], 3),
    `p-value` = format.pval(coefs[, "Pr(>|z|)"], digits = 4),
    `95% LCL` = round(cis[, 3], 4),
    `95% UCL` = round(cis[, 4], 4),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  knitr::kable(tbl, caption = caption, align = "lrrrrrrr", row.names = FALSE)
}








NoteHow to Read the Survival-Time Simulation





The simulation uses a simple piecewise hazard structure. Before Drug X starts, each patient has an untreated baseline hazard, lambda_base. After Drug X starts, the hazard becomes lambda_base * true_hr. Because true_hr = 0.70, treatment reduces the hazard to 70% of the untreated level.
The quantity log_u = -log(u) can be read as each patient’s randomly assigned cumulative hazard threshold. An event occurs when the cumulative hazard experienced by the patient reaches this threshold.
Before treatment starts, cumulative hazard accumulates at the untreated rate:
\[
\text{pre-treatment cumulative hazard} = \lambda_{\text{base}} \times t_{\text{init}}
\]
If log_u <= pre_treatment_hazard, the patient uses up their cumulative hazard threshold before treatment begins, so the event occurs during the untreated period:
\[
t_{\text{event}} = \frac{\text{log\_u}}{\lambda_{\text{base}}}
\]
If the patient survives until treatment initiation, only part of the cumulative hazard threshold has been used. The remaining hazard budget is:
\[
\text{log\_u} - \text{pre-treatment cumulative hazard}
\]
After treatment starts, hazard continues to accumulate, but at the lower treated rate, \(\lambda_{\text{base}} \times HR\). Therefore, the total event time is:
\[
t_{\text{event}} =
t_{\text{init}} +
\frac{\text{log\_u} - \text{pre-treatment cumulative hazard}}
{\lambda_{\text{base}} \times HR}
\]
In short, the code simulates a patient who first experiences untreated risk, then, if they live long enough to initiate Drug X, continues accumulating hazard at a lower treated rate.




4.1 Description of the Simulated Cohort
Before fitting any model, we inspect the simulated cohort. The key feature is that treatment is not assigned at time zero. Patients who eventually receive Drug X have a waiting period before their first recorded treatment start date.

  Metric = c(
    "Total patients",
    "Ever received Drug X during observed follow-up",
    "Observed deaths",
    "Mean age",
    "ECOG 1 proportion",

    "Median treatment initiation delay among treated (days)"

    nrow(df),
    sum(df$ever_treated),
    sprintf("%s (%.1f%%)", event_count, event_pct),

    sprintf("%.1f%%", mean(df$ecog == 1) * 100),
    sprintf("%.1f", median(df$time)),
    sprintf("%.1f", median(df$t_init_display[df$ever_treated == 1], na.rm = TRUE))
  )
)

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 5 Immortal Time Bias (ITB): Intuition and First Correction
text:
5 Immortal Time Bias (ITB): Intuition and First Correction

5.1 The Meditation & Longevity Paradox
Consider a study evaluating whether a 12-week intensive meditation course increases overall survival (OS):

Cohort: 1,000 participants followed for 5 years.
Exposure Group (\(Z=1\)): Completed the full 12-week program.
Control Group (\(Z=0\)): Did not complete the program (includes those who died or dropped out before week 12).
The Result: Participants who completed the course show a Hazard Ratio (\(HR\)) of 0.30 (70% risk reduction).3
The Error: Since a patient had to survive 12 weeks to complete the program, the meditation group is guaranteed 0% mortality during the first 12 weeks. Sicker patients who died in weeks 1–11 were automatically allocated to the control group.

3 Completion status at Week 12 is post-baseline information. It cannot be used retrospectively to define the baseline exposure group; otherwise, the first 12 weeks of survival are incorrectly credited to the intervention.

5.2 Landmark Analysis
Landmark Analysis is a classical approach to resolve this:

Select Landmark Time (\(T_L\)): E.g., Week 12.
Exclude Early Events: Exclude all patients who died or were censored before \(T_L\).
Re-classify: Classify survivors at \(T_L\) based on their exposure status at \(T_L\).
Follow-up: Set \(T_L\) as the new baseline (\(T_{start} = T_L\)) and follow patients from that point.


HTA Audit of Landmark Analysis

Pros: Simple, highly intuitive, and removes the immortal period.
Cons:

Information Loss: Discards all events and person-time before \(T_L\). If the drug has high early toxicity, this signal is completely lost.
Selection Bias: The populations at \(T_L\) may no longer be balanced, as sicker patients in the control group may have died, while sicker patients in the treated group were protected by the “immortal” definition.


Therefore, landmark analysis is usually better positioned as an intuitive diagnostic or sensitivity analysis, rather than the preferred primary analysis for HTA submissions. It is most defensible when the clinical question is explicitly conditional on surviving and remaining eligible until the landmark time; otherwise, time-varying exposure models or cloning-censoring-IPCW are generally more aligned with the original target trial question.



5.3 Applying Landmark Analysis to the Simulated Cohort
We now apply a Day 90 landmark analysis to the simulated Drug X cohort. Patients who died or were censored before Day 90 are excluded. Among those who remain under observation at Day 90, treatment status is re-defined based on whether Drug X had started by that date.

# Shift follow-up time so Day 90 becomes the new time zero

fit_landmark <- coxph(
  Surv(time_shifted, event) ~ treated_at_landmark + age + ecog,
  data = df_landmark
)

title: Survival Analysis & Immortal Time Bias in Real-World Evidence
section: 5 Immortal Time Bias in the Simulated Drug X Cohort
text:
5 Immortal Time Bias in the Simulated Drug X Cohort
This specific problem is known in epidemiology and survival analysis as Immortal Time Bias (ITB). The naive Cox result above illustrates the mechanism: survival time before Drug X initiation is incorrectly credited to the treated group because treatment status was defined using information observed after \(T_0\).
Now that the bias mechanism is visible, we evaluate three ways to handle delayed treatment initiation: landmark analysis, time-dependent Cox regression, and cloning-censoring-IPCW.

5.1 First Correction: Landmark Analysis
Landmark Analysis is a classical approach to resolve this:

Select Landmark Time (\(T_L\)): E.g., Day 90.
Exclude Early Events: Exclude all patients who died or were censored before \(T_L\).
Re-classify: Classify survivors at \(T_L\) based on their treatment status at \(T_L\).
Follow-up: Set \(T_L\) as the new baseline (\(T_{start} = T_L\)) and follow patients from that point.


HTA Audit of Landmark Analysis

Pros: Simple, highly intuitive, and removes the immortal period.
Cons:

Information Loss: Discards all events and person-time before \(T_L\). If the drug has high early toxicity, this signal is completely lost.
Selection Bias: The populations at \(T_L\) may no longer be balanced, as sicker patients in the control group may have died, while sicker patients in the treated group were protected by the “immortal” definition.
Arbitrary Landmark Choice: The selected landmark time is a design decision, not a statistical truth. If \(T_L\) is too early, many later initiators remain classified as untreated; if \(T_L\) is too late, more early events are discarded.


Therefore, landmark analysis is usually better positioned as an intuitive diagnostic or sensitivity analysis, rather than the preferred primary analysis for HTA submissions. It is most defensible when the clinical question is explicitly conditional on surviving and remaining eligible until the landmark time; otherwise, time-varying exposure models or cloning-censoring-IPCW are generally more aligned with the original target trial question.



5.2 Applying Landmark Analysis to the Simulated Cohort
